Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 39, verse 6:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses﴾

For each of these coverings (ḥujub) has a darkness specific to it. So Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the stages of His creation and His transferring it from one state to another within them. And He mentioned the darknesses of the coverings that are upon the fetus (janīn). The majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn) said:

They are the darkness of the abdomen, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (mashīma), since each of these is a covering over the fetus.

Others said: they are the darkness of the fathers' loins (aṣlāb al-ābā'), the darkness of the mothers' bellies, and the darkness of the placenta.

Weaker than this view is the view of those who said: the darkness of the night, the darkness of the belly, and the darkness of the womb, for night and day are the same with respect to the fetus.

Buqrāṭ (Hippocrates) said: when the woman conceives, she does not feel pain from the gathering of blood that descends and collects around her womb, nor does she feel weakness as she does when the menstrual flow (ṭamth) descends, because her blood does not surge every month; rather it descends into the womb little by little every day, a calm descent without pain. When it reaches the womb, the fetus is nourished by it and grows. Then he said: and not long after that, when flesh and body are created for the fetus, the coverings form; and as it grows, the coverings also grow, and they take on a cavity outside the fetus. When the blood descends from the mother, the fetus draws it and is nourished by it, so it increases in its flesh; and the bad blood, which is not fit for nourishment, descends into the channels of the coverings. Thus the coverings that, once they have a cavity, receive the blood are called the placenta.

And he said: when the fetus is complete and its form is perfected, and it draws the blood for its nourishment in the proper amount, the coverings expand and the placenta appears, which consists of the organs we mentioned. If its inner part expands, its outer part expands too, because it is more appropriate for that, since it has a place to which it extends.

He, glory be to Him, must be thanked, and He loves to be thanked, by reason, by revelation, and by natural disposition (fitrah). The obligation to thank Him is more evident than the obligation of any other obligation, and how could it not be obligatory for the servants to praise Him, affirm His oneness, love Him, mention His favours and His kindness, glorify and magnify Him, submit to Him, speak of His blessings, and acknowledge them by every means of obligation? Thanks is therefore the most beloved thing to Him and the greatest in reward. He created the creation, sent down the Books, and legislated the laws, and this entails creating the causes by which thanks becomes more perfect. Among them is that He differentiated among His servants in their outward and inward attributes, in their creation and character, their religions, their provisions, their livelihoods, and their life-spans.

When the healthy person sees the afflicted, the rich sees the poor, and the believer sees the disbeliever, his thanks to God grows greater, he recognises the worth of the blessing upon him and what He has specifically granted him and preferred him with over others, so his thanks, submission and acknowledgement of the blessing increase.

In a report that Imam Ahmad mentioned in al-Zuhd (asceticism): "Moses said: O Lord, why did You not make Your servants equal? He said: I wished to be thanked."

If it is said: Was it not possible for Him to make them equal in blessings and equal in thanks, as He did with the angels?

It is said: Had He done that, the thanks that resulted would have been of a different kind from the thanks that results in this manner, and thanks given in response to preference and distinction is higher and better than other thanks. This is why the thanks, submission and humility of the angels before His greatness and majesty, after they witnessed what happened to Iblis and what happened to Harut and Marut, was higher and more complete than what came before.

This is the wisdom of the Lord. This is why the thanks of the prophets and their followers, after they beheld the destruction of their enemies and the Lord's vengeance upon them and the might He sent down upon them, was higher and more complete.

Likewise the thanks of the people of Paradise in Paradise, as they watch His enemies who denied His messengers and associated others with Him undergoing that punishment. Without doubt their thanks, their contentment and their love for their Lord at that time are more complete and greater than if all creation were to share in the bliss. The love that arises in His friends for Him, and their contentment and thanks, as they see the opposite of it in their own kind in every respect, is more perfect and complete.

Opposites reveal the beauty of one another, and by their opposites things are made clear. Had the ugly not been created, the virtue of beauty and goodliness would not be known; had darkness not been created, the virtue of light would not be known; had the various kinds of affliction not been created, the worth of well-being would not be known; had Hell not existed, the worth of Paradise would not be known. Had God, glory be to Him, made the day perpetual, its worth would not be known; had He made the night perpetual, its worth would not be known. The people most aware of the worth of a blessing are those who have tasted affliction, and the most aware of the worth of poverty are those who have suffered the bitter trials of poverty and need. Had all people been of one form of beauty, the worth of beauty would not be known; likewise, had they all been believers, the worth of faith and the blessing of it would not be known. Blessed is He, whose creation and command are governed by perfect wisdom and abundant favours; this clarifies it.

(Question)

If it is said: Does the Lord, glory be to Him, approve of what He has decreed of disbelief, wickedness and disobedience in any way whatsoever?

It is said: This matter is more difficult than the previous one.

Many of the Ash'aris, indeed most of them, and those who follow them, say that approval, love and will in relation to the Lord, exalted is He, have one meaning, and that whatever He wills and desires He loves and approves. Then they raised this question against themselves and answered that it is not impossible to say that He approves of them, but not in a specific sense; rather it is said that He approves of everything He created, decreed and determined, and we do not single out the blameworthy matters from that, just as it is said: He is the Lord of everything, but one does not say: the Lord of such-and-such, for base and lowly things.

This is their explicit statement that He is in fact pleased with them, and that the unrestricted expression was only avoided out of courtesy and reverence. When they were confronted with His words: ﴿He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, they answered it with two responses:

One: it refers to one who does not commit it; as for one who does commit it, He approves of it, since it occurs by His will and desire.

Two: He does not approve it for them as a religion, meaning He does not legislate it for them or command them to it, but He approves it from them in the sense of His universal decree (kawnan). According to their view the meaning of the verse becomes: He does not approve disbelief for His servants insofar as it does not exist among them; but if it exists among them, He loves it and approves it. This is, as you see, utterly false and corrupt, and He, glory be to Him, has informed that He does not approve what exists of that, even though it occurs by His will, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He is with them when they plot by night what He does not approve of in speech﴾. This is a saying that occurs by His will and decree, and yet He has informed that He does not approve of it.

Likewise His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾. He, glory be to Him, does not love it, either in the universal sense or in the religious sense, even though it occurs by His decree, just as He does not love Iblis and his hosts, or Pharaoh and his party, though He is their Lord and Creator. Whoever makes love and approval mean will and desire must hold that Allah, glory be to Him, loves Iblis, his hosts, Pharaoh, Haman, Qarun and all the disbelievers, their disbelief, the oppressors and their deeds. This, just as it contradicts the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus known by necessity, also contradicts the natural disposition upon which the peoples of the worlds were created, which has not been altered by the agreement and mutual exhortation of false sayings.

He, glory be to Him, has informed that He abhors many actions, hates them, dislikes them and is angered by them. He said: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed; indeed it was an abomination and hatred and an evil way﴾. He said: ﴿That is because they followed what displeased Allah﴾. He said: ﴿Great is their hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾. He said: ﴿But Allah disliked their setting out, so He held them back﴾, and it is impossible to interpret this dislike as anything other than religious dislike in the sense of command, since He commanded them to jihad. He said: ﴿All of that, its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾. Thus He has informed that He dislikes, hates, abhors, is angered by, opposes and blames, and curses; and it is impossible that He loves that or is pleased with it. He, glory be to Him, dislikes it and is exalted above loving it or being pleased with it. Indeed that does not befit His servant either, for it is a deficiency and defect in the created being that he should love corruption, evil, injustice, transgression and disbelief and be pleased with them. How then can such a thing be attributed to Allah, blessed and exalted?

This principle is among the greatest errors committed by many of those who affirm predestination, and their error in it is equal to, or worse than, the error of those who deny predestination. Because of it the deniers gained power over them, persisted in the ugliness of their saying, and magnified the censure against them for it.

These ones say He loves disbelief, wickedness, disobedience, injustice, transgression and corruption; those ones say that it does not fall under His will, power and creation; those ones say that nothing exists in His dominion except what He loves and approves; and these ones say that what He does not will exists in His dominion, and that He wills what does not exist.

Glory be to Allah, exalted far above what both groups say. All praise is due to Allah, who guided us to what He sent His Messenger with, sent down His Book with, and created His servants upon, and who cleared us of the innovations of these and those. So to Him belong praise, favour, grace, blessing and good commendation. We ask Him for success in what He loves and approves, and that He keep us away from misleading innovations and trials.

(Section)

If you say: How can Allah, glory be to Him, will a matter that He does not approve of or love? And how does He will it and bring it into being? And how can His willing it and His hatred and dislike of it come together?

It is said: This is the very question over which people have split into sects, and their methods and sayings have diverged on account of it.

Know that what is willed is of two kinds: what is willed for its own sake, and what is willed for something else.

That which is willed for its own sake is sought and loved for its own essence and for the good in it. This is the object of the will of ends and purposes.

That which is willed for something else may not in itself be an aim for the one who wills it, nor does it contain benefit for him when considered in its own essence, though it is a sought and willed means. It is disliked by him in respect of its own self and essence, yet willed by him in respect of its leading to and bringing him to what he wills. Both matters come together in it: his hatred of it and his will for it, and they are not contradictory, because their objects differ. This is like a medicine that is extremely disagreeable, when the one who takes it knows that his cure lies in it; or like amputating a rotting limb when one knows that the preservation of the body lies in cutting it off; or like traversing a very arduous distance when one knows that it brings him to his desire and beloved. Indeed the intelligent person, in choosing and willing this disliked thing, suffices with a dominant assumption, even if its outcome is hidden from him and its consequence concealed; how much more so one for whom consequences are not hidden? He, glory be to Him, dislikes a thing and hates it in its essence, and this does not contradict His willing it for something else, and its being a cause of what is more beloved to Him than its absence.

An example of this: He, glory be to Him, created Iblis, who is the substance of the corruption of religions, deeds, beliefs and wills, and is the cause of the wretchedness of the servants and of their acting in ways that anger the Lord, blessed and exalted is He. He is the one who strives to bring about the opposite of what Allah loves and approves, by every path and every stratagem. Thus he is hated by the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, and abhorred by Him. Allah has cursed him, hated him and been angry with him. Yet despite this, he is a means to many beloved things to the Lord, exalted, that are consequences of his creation, whose existence is more beloved to Him than their non-existence.

Among them: that the servants may see the power of the Lord, exalted, to create opposites and contraries. So He created this essence, which is the most wicked and evil of essences and the cause of all evil, in contrast to the essence of Gabriel, which is the noblest, purest and most pure-hearted of essences and the substance of all good. Blessed is Allah, the Creator of this and that. Likewise His complete power became manifest to them in the creation of night and day, light and darkness, illness and cure, life and death, heat and cold, beauty and ugliness, earth and heaven, male and female, water and fire, good and evil.

This is among the clearest proofs of the perfection of His power, might, sovereignty and dominion. For He created these opposites, set some against others, made some dominant over others, and made them the loci of His governance, management and wisdom. Thus the emptiness of existence of some of them entirely would be a nullification of His wisdom and of the perfection of His management and the governance of His kingdom.

Among them: the manifestation of the effects of His names of subjugation, such as the Subduer (al-Qahhar), the Avenger (al-Muntaqim), the Just (al-'Adl), the Harmer (al-Darr), the Severe in punishment (Shadid al-'Iqab), the Swift in reckoning (Sari' al-Hisab), the Possessor of mighty seizure (Dhu al-Batsh al-Shadid), the Abaser (al-Khafid), and the Humiliator (al-Mudhill). These names and actions are perfections, so the existence of their objects is necessary. Had all creation been of the nature of an angel, the effects of these names and actions would not have appeared.

Among them: the manifestation of the effects of His names that include His forbearance, pardon, forgiveness, concealment, overlooking of His due right, and freeing of whomever He wills of His servants. Had there not been the creation of what He dislikes of the causes that lead to the manifestation of the effects of these names, these wisdoms and benefits would have been nullified. The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated this when he said: "Were you not to sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin and then seek Allah's forgiveness, and He would forgive them."

Among them: the manifestation of the effects of the names of wisdom and expertise. He, glory be to Him, is the All-Wise, the All-Aware, who places things in their proper places and sets them in their fitting stations. He does not place a thing in other than its place, nor set it in other than the station required by the perfection of His knowledge, wisdom and expertise. He does not place deprivation and withholding in the place of giving and bounty, nor bounty and giving in the place of deprivation and withholding; nor reward in the place of punishment, nor punishment in the place of reward; nor lowering in the place of elevating, nor elevating in the place of lowering; nor honour in the place of humiliation, nor humiliation in the place of honour; nor does He command what should be forbidden, nor forbid what should be commanded.

He knows best where to place His message, and best who is fit to accept it, and He thanks him for reaching it and for its arrival to him. He knows best who is not fit for that and does not deserve it. He is too wise to withhold it from its people or to place it with those who are not its people.

Had the disliked and hateful causes been supposed to be absent, these effects would have been nullified and would not have appeared to His creation, and the wisdoms and interests consequent upon them would have been lost. The loss of these is worse than the occurrence of those causes.

If those causes were to be nullified because of the evil in them, then the good that is greater than the evil in those causes would be nullified. This is like the sun, the rain and the winds, which contain benefits many times over what harm and damage results from them. Were their nullification supposed, so that no partial evil would result from them, then good greater than that evil would be lost, by an incomparable measure.

(Section)

Among them: the realisation of the diverse servitude that would not have come about had Iblis not been created, and only some of it would have been realised rather than all of it.

For the servitude of jihad is among the most beloved kinds of servitude to Him, glory be to Him. Had all people been believers, this servitude and its consequences would have been nullified: loyalty for His sake, enmity for His sake, love for His sake and hatred for His sake; the giving of one's self to Him in fighting His enemy; the servitude of enjoining good and forbidding evil; the servitude of patience and opposing one's desire; and preferring the beloveds of the Lord over the beloveds of the self.

Among them: the servitude of repentance, returning to Him and seeking His forgiveness. For He, glory be to Him, loves those who repent and loves their repentance. Had the causes from which one repents been nullified, the servitude of repentance and seeking forgiveness from them would have been nullified.

Among them: the servitude of opposing His enemy, defying him for Allah's sake, and enraging him for Allah's sake. This is among the most beloved kinds of servitude to Him, for He, glory be to Him, loves that His friend should enrage His enemy, defy him and cause him distress. This is a servitude that none perceives except the astute.

Among them: that one worships Him by seeking refuge from His enemy and asking Him to protect him from him and to preserve him from his plotting and harm.

Among them: that His servants' fear and caution become intense when they see what befell His enemy through his opposition, and his fall from the angelic rank to the satanic rank. Thus they do not give themselves over to the deception of hope after that.

Among its benefits: they obtain the reward of opposing Satan and being hostile to him, the attainment of which is conditional upon enmity and opposition to him. Most acts of worship of the heart and the limbs are therefore ordained upon opposing him.

Among its benefits: taking him as an enemy is itself one of the greatest and most exalted kinds of servitude. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir: 6]. Thus, taking him as an enemy is the most beneficial thing for the servant, and it is beloved to the Lord.

Among its benefits: the human nature comprises good and evil, and the pure and the impure. This is latent within it, like fire latent in the flint. Satan was created to draw out what is in the natures of the people of evil from potential into action, and the Messengers were sent to draw out what is in the nature of the people of good from potential into action. The Most Wise of the wise thus draws out what is in the faculties of those (the people of good) of the good latent within them, so that its effects are realised, and what is in the faculties of the others of evil, so that its effects are realised, and His wisdom is manifested regarding both groups, His judgment is executed upon both, and what was known to Him is made manifest, in accordance with His prior knowledge.

This is the question which His angels asked when they said: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. The angels thought that the existence of one who glorifies Him with His praise, obeys Him and worships Him was more fitting than the existence of one who disobeys Him and opposes Him. So He, glorified is He, answered them that He knows of the wisdoms, the benefits and the praiseworthy ends in the creation of this kind what the angels do not know.

Among its benefits: the manifestation of many of His signs and wondrous works came about through the occurrence of disbelief and polytheism from disbelieving, wrongdoing souls, such as the sign of the Flood, the sign of the wind, the sign of the destruction of Thamud and the people of Lut, the sign of the fire being transformed into coolness and safety for Ibrahim, and the signs which Allah the Exalted performed at the hand of Musa, and other of His signs, after mentioning each of which He, glorified is He, says in Surah ash-Shu'ara': ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers. And indeed your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Most Merciful﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 8]. Had it not been for the disbelief of the disbelievers and the obstinacy of the deniers, these resplendent signs, which people speak of generation after generation until eternity, would not have become manifest.

Among its benefits: the creation of opposing causes, where some of them overpower and defeat others, is part of the perfection of Lordship, of all-pervasive power, of complete wisdom and of perfect dominion, and although the perfection of Lordship is complete in itself, even had these causes not been created, yet creating them is among the necessary requirements of His perfection, dominion, power and wisdom. The manifestation of their influence and rulings in the world of observation is therefore a realisation of that perfection and one of its necessary demands. Thus the filling of the levels of the unseen and the observable with the rulings of the attributes is one of the effects of the absolute divine perfection in all its aspects, divisions and ends.

In summary: servitude, the signs and the wondrous works that are the consequences of creating what He does not love nor approve of, and of His decree and will, are more beloved to Him, glorified and exalted is He, than their being lost and nullified by nullifying their causes.

If you say: Was it possible for those wisdoms to exist without these causes?

I say: This is a false question, for it is the supposition of the existence of the necessitated without its necessary consequence, like supposing the existence of a son without a father, motion without the one who moves, or repentance without the one who repents.

If you say: If these causes are willed because of the wisdoms they lead to, are they then pleasing and beloved from this aspect, or are they hateful from all aspects?

I say: This question arises from two angles.

The first: from the perspective of the Lord, glorified and exalted is He. Is He loving of them from the standpoint of their leading to what He loves, even though He hates them in themselves?

The second: from the perspective of the servant, namely whether it is permissible for him to be content with them from that aspect as well. This is a question of considerable importance.

Know that all evil returns to non-existence, meaning the absence of good and of its causes that lead to it, and from this aspect it is evil. As for its pure existence, there is no evil in it.

An example: the existence of evil souls is good insofar as they exist. Evil only came to them by cutting off the substance of good from them. For they were created originally as moving and not still. If they are aided with knowledge and the inspiration of good, they move towards it. If they are left, they move by their nature towards its opposite, and their movement, insofar as it is movement, is a good. It is only evil in relation, not insofar as it is movement. And all evil is injustice, which is placing a thing in other than its place. Were it placed in its proper place, it would not be evil.

Thus it is known that the aspect of evil in it is a relative relation. For this reason, the punishments placed in their proper locations are good in themselves, although they are evil in relation to the place upon which they fall, because of the pain they cause, for the nature was receptive to its opposite, pleasure, and disposed towards it. So that pain becomes evil in relation to it. Yet it is good in relation to the Agent, in that He placed it in its place. Indeed, He, glorified is He, does not create pure evil from all aspects and considerations, for His wisdom rejects that. Rather, that created thing may be evil and corrupt in some considerations, while its creation contains benefits and wisdoms in other considerations which outweigh the corruptions. Indeed, reality is confined to this. It is not possible with regard to the Real, majestic is His majesty, that He wills a thing which is corruption from every aspect in every consideration, with no benefit in its creation in any way. This is among the most manifest impossibilities. For He, glorified is He, holds good in His hand, and evil does not belong to Him. Rather, everything that belongs to Him is good. Evil only arises through the absence of this relation and connection to Him. Had it belonged to Him, it would not be evil. So reflect on this. The severing of its relation to Him is what made it evil.

If you say: Has its relation to Him not been severed in creation and will?

I say: From this aspect it is not evil, for its existence is what is attributed to Him, and from this aspect it is not evil. The evil within it is from the absence of His providing it with good and its causes, and absence is not a thing, so that it could be attributed to the One in whose hand is good.

If you wish further clarification of this, know that the causes of good are three: bringing into existence, preparing, and providing. These are the goods and their causes.

The bringing into existence of a cause is good, and it belongs to Allah. Its preparation is good, and it also belongs to Him. Its provision is good, and it also belongs to Him.

When no preparation or provision occurs in it, evil arises in it through this absence, which does not belong to the Agent. Rather, its opposite belongs to Him.

If you say: Why did He not provide it when He brought it into existence?

I say: Wisdom did not require bringing it into existence and providing it. He, glorified is He, brings into existence and provides. What wisdom required was bringing it into existence while not providing it, so He brought it into existence by His wisdom and did not provide it by His wisdom. Its bringing into existence is good, and the evil occurred from its not being provided.

If you say: Why did He not provide all existents?

I say: This is a corrupt question, one whose asker supposes that equality among existents is more eloquent in wisdom. This is sheer ignorance. Rather, all wisdom lies in this enormous variation found among them. There is no variation in the creation of each kind among them, for in the creation of each kind there is no variation. Variation only occurs through non-existential matters, which creation did not involve. Otherwise there is no variation in creation.

If this proves difficult for you and you do not grasp it properly, then refer to the saying of the poet:

؎ If you are unable to do something, leave it, and move on to what you are able to do.

As it is mentioned that al-Asma'i met al-Khalil ibn Ahmad and was keen to understand prosody from him, but he could not manage it. Al-Khalil said to him one day: "Scan this verse for me," and recited to him: "If you are unable to do something..." (the verse), and he understood what he meant. So he gave up on it and did not occupy himself with it.

The secret of the matter: contentment with Allah entails contentment with His attributes, His acts, His names and His rulings, but it does not entail contentment with all of His created effects. Rather, the reality of servitude is that the servant agrees with Him in His pleasure and His displeasure, so he is pleased with what He is pleased with, and displeased with what He is displeased with.

If it is said: He, glorified is He, is pleased with the punishment of one who deserves punishment, so how can the servant be pleased with His punishing him?

It is said: If he agreed with Him in His pleasure with His punishment, it would turn into delight and joy. But this does not occur from him.

For he does not agree with Him in His love and obedience, which are the joy of the soul, the coolness of the eye and the life of the heart. How then could he agree with Him in His love for punishment, which is the most hateful thing to him and the most burdensome thing upon him? Rather, he was averse to what He loves of obedience and monotheism. So he is not content with what He chooses of punishment. Had he accepted that, the punishment would have been lifted from him.

If you say: How does contentment with the decree that the servant dislikes, such as sickness, poverty and pain, coexist with his aversion to it?

I say: There is no contradiction in that. He is pleased with it from the aspect that it leads to what he loves, and he dislikes it from the aspect that it causes him pain, like a bitter medicine which he knows contains his cure. Thus his contentment with it and his aversion to it coexist.

If you say: How can He be pleased for His servant with something without helping him to it?

I say: Because helping him to it may entail the loss of something He loves more greatly than the attainment of that obedience which He was pleased with for him. And the occurrence of that obedience from him may include a corruption that is more hateful to Him, glorified is He, than His love for that obedience, such that its occurrence from him would necessitate a dominant corruption and forfeit a dominant benefit. Exalted is He, has indicated this in His saying: ﴿Had they wished to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation. But Allah was averse to their being sent forth, so He held them back, and it was said: "Remain with those who remain." Had they gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption, and they would have hurried through your ranks, seeking to cause you fitnah, and among you are those who listen to them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ [at-Tawbah: 46-47]. He, glorified is He, informed that He disliked their being sent forth with His Messenger ﷺ for the expedition, though it is an act of obedience and nearness, and He had commanded them to it. When He disliked it from them, He held them back from it. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the corruptions that would have resulted from their going out had they gone forth with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption﴾ [at-Tawbah: 47], that is, corruption and evil; ﴿and they would have hurried through your ranks﴾ [at-Tawbah: 47], that is, they would have sought among you to spread corruption and evil; ﴿seeking to cause you fitnah, and among you are those who listen to them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 47], that is, those who accept from them and respond to them. From the combination of these people's striving for corruption and those people's acceptance of them, there would arise evil greater than the benefit of their going out. Thus wisdom and mercy required that He prevent them from going out and keep them from it.

So take this example as a foundation for this chapter, and measure other matters by it.

If you say: This may be conceived for me regarding the Lord's pleasure with some of what He creates from one aspect and His dislike of it from another aspect. How then can both matters be combined in my case with respect to sins and transgressions?

I say: This is conceivable and possible, indeed it occurs. The servant detests and hates that, and dislikes it insofar as it was done by him, was caused by him, occurs through his acquisition, will and choice. And he is pleased with Allah's knowledge, His decree, His will and His universal permission regarding it. So he is pleased with what Allah has bestowed, and displeased with what proceeds from himself. This is the path of a group among the people of gnosis.

Another group saw that dislike of that is absolute, and non-contentment with it from every aspect.

These in reality do not oppose those. For when the servant dislikes it absolutely, the dislike falls only upon the aspect of it which is disliked. These did not dislike the Lord's knowledge, His decree, His will, and His binding of His universal judgment, and those were not pleased with it from the aspect for which the Lord was displeased with it and hated it.

The crux of the matter is this: whatever in these things is attributed to the Lord is not hateful, while whatever in them is attributed to the servant is what is hateful and displeasing.

If you say: "Nothing of these things is attributed to the servant?"

I say: This is the false compulsion (jabr), which prevents its adherent from escaping this narrow position. The Qadari (Qadariyya, those who affirm human free will to the exclusion of divine decree) is closer to escaping it than the Jabari (Jabriyya, those who deny human agency and affirm only compulsion). The Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), who stand in the middle between the Qadariyya and the Jabriyya, are the most fortunate of the two groups in escaping it.

If you say: "How can regret and repentance (tawbah) occur while witnessing wisdom in the divine decree and witnessing the all-sustaining (al-qayyumiyyah) and the all-pervading will?"

I say: This is what has led one whose insight is blinded, in witnessing the command, to see it contrary to what it is. He sees those acts as acts of obedience because his will agrees with the divine will and decree in them, and he says: "If I disobey His command, I have indeed obeyed His will in that." And it has been said:

"I have become subject to what He chooses for me,
so all my actions are acts of obedience."

These are the most blind of creatures in insight, and the most ignorant of God and His religious (dini) and cosmic (kawni) rulings. Obedience is conformity to the command, not conformity to the decree and the will. Had conformity to the decree been obedience to God, Iblis would have been among the greatest of those obedient to God. The people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and the people of Pharaoh would all have been obedient to Him, and He would then have punished them with the severest punishment for their obedience and taken vengeance upon them for it. This is the utmost ignorance of God, His names, His attributes and His acts.

If you say: "Along with that, then combine for me regret and repentance with the witnessing of the all-sustaining and of wisdom?"

I say: When the servant witnesses the powerlessness of his self, the effectiveness of the decrees upon him, his utter need for his Lord, and his lack of independence from His protection and preservation even for the blink of an eye, he is in this state with God, not with himself. The commission of sin by him therefore cannot possibly occur in this state at all, for upon him is a strong fortress of: "By Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he strikes, by Me he walks." Sin cannot be conceived from him in this state. But when he is veiled from this witnessing, falls down to his natural existence (wujud tabi'i), and remains with his self, then the rule of the self, nature and passion takes control over him. This natural existence is one in which snares and traps have been set, and hunters have been released against it. He must fall into one of those snares and one of those traps. This existence is a veil between him and his Lord, and at that point the veil descends, the motive grows stronger, and the restraint weakens. The darkness intensifies, the faculties weaken, and how can he then escape those traps and snares? But when the mist of that natural existence clears, its darkness is lifted, its gloom dispelled, and you go away from your self and nature toward your Lord:

"A secret has appeared to you whose concealment was long from you,
and a dawn has risen whose darkness you yourself were."

"If you are absent from it, it settles within you, and its tents are pitched
upon the shoulder of the guarded unveiling."

"You are the veil of the heart from the secret of its Unseen,
and were it not for you, no seal would have been set upon it."

"A discourse whose hearing never wearies,
sweet to us, its prose and its verse."

"When the self mentions it, its toil ceases,
and the dust that troubled the heart is removed."

At that point there come into his presence regret, repentance and turning back (inabah). For he was in disobedience with his self, veiled therein from his Lord and from His obedience. When he departs from that existence and passes into another existence, he remains with his Lord, not with his self.

When this is understood, repentance and regret take place in this existence in which he is with his Lord. This does not contradict the witnessing of wisdom and the all-sustaining; rather, it coexists with it and draws its strength from it. And success is from God.

His words: "It is valid only with three conditions: that the states are equal for the servant; that the enmity with the creation is removed; and that he is freed from asking and insistence."

Meaning: contentment with God is only realized through these three matters. The contentment that conforms to God's decree is one in which the states, of blessing and of affliction, are equal in his acceptance of God's good choice for him.

It does not mean that these states are equal for him in what is agreeable and disagreeable to him, for that is contrary to human nature, indeed contrary to animal nature.

Nor does it mean that the states are equal for him in obedience and disobedience, for that contradicts servanthood in every respect. Rather, blessing and affliction are equal for him in being content with both, for several reasons:

The first: he has entrusted himself (mufawwad). The one who has entrusted himself is content with whatever the one to whom he entrusted himself chooses for him, especially when he knows the perfection of His wisdom, His mercy, His gentleness and His good choice for him.

The second: he is certain that there is no alteration of God's words and no reverser of His judgment, and that what God wills comes to be and what He does not will does not come to be. He knows that each of affliction and blessing is by a prior decree and an inescapable destiny.

The third: he is a pure servant, and a pure servant does not resent the operation of the rulings of his master who is compassionate, righteous, sincere and benevolent. Rather, he receives all of them with contentment in Him and from Him.

The fourth: he is a lover, and the true lover is one who is content with whatever his beloved treats him with.

The fifth: he is ignorant of the outcomes of affairs, while his master knows best what is good for him and what benefits him.

The sixth: he does not desire the good of his self in every respect, even if he knew its causes. He is ignorant and wrongdoing. But his Lord, exalted is He, desires his good and drives to him its causes. Among the greatest of its causes is what the servant dislikes, for his good in what he dislikes is many times over his good in what he loves. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing and Allah makes in it much good.﴾ [al-Nisa': 19].

The seventh: he is a Muslim (muslim). The Muslim is one who has surrendered himself to God, has not objected to the operation of His rulings upon him, and has not resented that.

The eighth: he is one who knows his Lord, has good opinion of Him, and does not accuse Him regarding what He brings upon him of decrees and destinies. His good opinion of Him necessitates for him the equality of states and his contentment with what his master, glorified is He, chooses for him.

The ninth: he knows that his share of what is decreed is what he receives with it of contentment or resentment. He cannot avoid it. If he is content, he has contentment; if he resents, he has resentment.

The tenth: his knowledge that if he is content, it becomes for him a blessing and a gift, its burden lightens upon him, and he is helped to bear it. If he resents it, its weight multiplies upon him and exhausts him, and it increases only in severity. Even if resentment availed him anything, there would be in it a comfort for him more beneficial to him than contentment with it.

The essence of the matter: his belief that the decree of the Lord, exalted is He, is good for him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, Allah does not decree for a believer a decree except that it is good for him. If prosperity befalls him, he gives thanks, and it is good for him; and if adversity befalls him, he is patient, and it is good for him. And this is only for the believer."

The eleventh: that he knows that the completeness of his servanthood lies in the operation upon him of what he dislikes of the rulings. Were nothing of them to operate upon him except what he loves, he would be the furthest thing from the servanthood of his Lord. His servanthood is not complete, in patience, reliance, contentment, humble supplication, need, abasement, submission and others, except through the operation of the decree upon him with what he dislikes. The matter is not contentment with the decree that accords with one's nature; rather, the matter is the painful decree that is contrary to one's nature.

The twelfth: that he knows his contentment with his Lord, glorified and exalted is He, in all states brings about the contentment of his Lord with him. When he is content with little sustenance, his Lord is content with him for little deed. When he is content with Him in all states and they are equal for him, he finds Him swiftest of all to be pleased with him when he seeks His pleasure and courts Him.

The thirteenth: that he knows his greatest comfort, joy and bliss lie in contentment with his Lord, exalted and sanctified is He, in all states. For contentment is the greatest gate of God, the resting place of the knowers, and the paradise of this world. It is fitting for one who sincerely advises his soul that his desire for it be intense, and that he not exchange it for anything else.

The fourteenth: that resentment is the gate of worry, grief and sorrow, dispersion of the heart, dimming of mind, evil condition, and thinking of God other than what He deserves. Contentment saves him from all of that and opens for him the gate of the paradise of this world before the paradise of the Hereafter.

The fifteenth: that contentment brings him tranquility, coolness of heart, its calm and its settling. Resentment brings about agitation of the heart, its doubt, its disquiet and its lack of settling.

The sixteenth: that contentment sends down upon him the tranquility (sakinah), than which there is nothing more beneficial for him. When tranquility descends upon him, he becomes steadfast, his conditions are set right, and his mind is set right. Resentment distances him from it according to its paucity or abundance. When tranquility departs from him, joy, security, ease, comfort and goodness of life depart with it. So among the greatest of God's blessings upon His servant is the descent of tranquility upon him, and among the greatest of its causes is contentment with Him in all states.

The seventeenth: that contentment opens for him the gate of safety, making his heart sound, pure from deceit, treachery and rancor. None is saved from God's punishment except one who comes to God with a sound heart. Likewise, the soundness of the heart is impossible with resentment and non-contentment. The more content the servant is, the sounder his heart. Corruption, treachery and deceit are the companions of resentment, while soundness of heart, its piety and its sincere counsel are the companions of contentment. Likewise envy is among the fruits of resentment, and the soundness of the heart from it is among the fruits of contentment.

The eighteenth: that resentment brings about the servant's fickleness and his lack of steadfastness with God, for he is content only with what suits his nature and self. Decrees continually operate with what suits him and with what does not suit him, and whenever there operates upon him of them what does not suit him, it angers him. Thus no foot stands firm for him in servanthood. When he is content with his Lord in all states, his foot is established in the station of servanthood. Nothing removes fickleness from the servant like contentment.

The nineteenth: that resentment opens for him the gate of doubt about God, His decree, His destiny, His wisdom and His knowledge. Rarely is the resentful one safe from a doubt that enters his heart and penetrates it, even if he does not perceive it. Had he searched his self with the utmost searching, he would find his certainty flawed and tainted. For contentment and certainty are two brothers who go together, while doubt and resentment are companions. This is the meaning of the hadith in al-Tirmidhi, or elsewhere: "If you are able to act with contentment together with certainty, do so. And if you are not able, then in patience upon what the self dislikes there is much good."

The twentieth: that contentment with what is decreed is among the happiness of the son of Adam, and his resentment is among his wretchedness, as in the Musnad and al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (raḍiyallahu 'anhu), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "From the happiness of the son of Adam is his seeking of God's guidance (istikharah) of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. And from the happiness of the son of Adam is his contentment with what Allah has decreed. And from the wretchedness of the son of Adam is his resentment of what Allah has decreed. And from the wretchedness of the son of Adam is his abandoning the seeking of Allah's guidance." Thus contentment with the decree is among the causes of happiness, and resentment against the decree is among the causes of wretchedness.

The twenty-first: that contentment necessitates for him that he not grieve over what has escaped him, nor rejoice in what has been given to him. That is among the best of faith. As for not grieving over what is lost, it is evident. As for not rejoicing in what has been given to him, it is because he knows that the calamity in it was written before its occurrence. How can he rejoice in something in which he knows there is an awaited calamity, inevitably?

The twenty-second: that whoever fills his heart with contentment with the decree, God fills his breast with richness, security and contentment, and empties his heart for His love, for turning to Him and for relying upon Him. Whoever misses his share of contentment, his heart is filled with the opposite of that, and he is occupied away from what his happiness and success lie in.

Contentment (ridā) empties the heart for God, while discontent (suhṭ) empties the heart of God.

The twenty-third: Contentment produces gratitude (shukr), which is among the highest stations of faith, indeed it is the reality of faith. Discontent produces its opposite, which is ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-ni'am), and may sometimes produce ingratitude toward the Benefactor (kufr al-mun'im). So when the servant is content with his Lord in all circumstances, this obliges gratitude to Him, and he becomes among those who are content and grateful. When contentment escapes him, he becomes among the discontented, and he treads the path of the disbelievers.

The twenty-fourth: Contentment removes from him the afflictions of greed (ḥirṣ) and avid craving (kalab) for this world, and that is the head of every sin, the root of every calamity, and the foundation of every ruin. So his contentment with his Lord in all circumstances removes from him the source of these afflictions.

The twenty-fifth: Satan mostly gains mastery over a person at the time of discontent and desire. There he hunts him. This is especially so when his discontent becomes firmly established, for he then says what does not please the Lord, does what does not please Him, and intends what does not please Him. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said at the death of his son Ibrahim: "The heart grieves, the eye sheds tears, and we say only what pleases the Lord." The death of children is among the circumstances that obligate the servant to discontent with the decree (qadar).

So the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that he would not say, in such a station, which most people find hateful, and so they speak what does not please God and do what does not please Him, anything but what pleases his Lord, blessed and exalted is He. For this reason, when the son of al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ died, he was seen laughing at the funeral. It was said to him: "Do you laugh when your son has died?" He said: "God has issued a decree, and I wished to be content with His decree."

A group denounced this statement of al-Fuḍayl and said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) wept on the day his son died, and he reported that 'the heart grieves and the eye sheds tears,' and he was at the highest stations of contentment. How then can this be counted among al-Fuḍayl's virtues?"

The verification is that the heart of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was broad enough to embrace the full completion of all ranks: contentment with God, and weeping out of mercy for the child. So he had the station of contentment and the station of mercy and tenderness of heart. Al-Fuḍayl's heart did not have the breadth to hold both the station of contentment and the station of mercy, so the two were not combined for him. People in this matter are on four levels.

The first: one in whom contentment with the decree and mercy toward the child are combined, so his eyes shed tears out of mercy while his heart is content.

The second: one whom contentment makes oblivious to mercy, so his heart is not broad enough for both matters; rather one of them makes him oblivious to the other.

The third: one whom mercy and tenderness make oblivious to contentment, so he does not witness it, rather he is annihilated from contentment.

The fourth: one who has neither contentment nor mercy. His grief is only over the loss of his share from the deceased. This is the state of most of creation. So there is no goodness, and no contentment with the Merciful. And God is the One sought for help.

So the first is at the highest rank of contentment, the second is below it, the third below the second, and the fourth is the discontented one.

The twenty-sixth: Contentment is choosing what God has chosen for His servant, and discontent is disliking what God has chosen for him, and this is a kind of hostility (muḥādda) to God. One is not freed from it except by contentment with God in all circumstances.

The twenty-seventh: Contentment expels desire (hawā) from the heart. The content person's desire follows the purpose of his Lord for him, meaning the purpose that his Lord loves and approves. Contentment and the following of desire never combine in the heart, ever. And if there is a share of this and a share of that, it is for whichever of the two predominates over it.

The twenty-eighth: Contentment with God in all circumstances produces God's contentment with the servant, as has already been explained in the discussion of being content with Him, for the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. There is an Israelite report that Moses (ﷺ) asked his Lord, mighty and majestic: "What brings me near to Your contentment?" He said: "My contentment lies in your contentment with My decree."

The twenty-ninth: Contentment with the decree is the hardest thing on the self (nafs). Indeed, it is in reality its slaughter, for it opposes its desire, its nature, and its will. It never becomes at rest (muṭma'inna) until it is content with the decree. Then it deserves to be told: "O soul at rest, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing; enter among My servants and enter My Paradise" (Q. al-Fajr 89:27–30).

The thirtieth: The content person receives his Lord's commands, both religious and decreed, with openness (inshirāḥ), submission (taslīm), good cheer of soul, and surrender. The discontented one receives them in the opposite manner, except for what agrees with his nature and his will regarding them.

We have already explained that contentment with that does not benefit him, nor is he rewarded for it, for he was not content with it because God decreed it, decreed it and commanded it, but he was content with it only because it agreed with his desire and his nature. So he was content only for himself and about himself, not for his Lord and not with his Lord.

The thirty-first: All transgressions have their root in lack of contentment, and all acts of obedience have their root in contentment. This is truly known only by one who knows the attributes of his own self and what arises from it of obedience and disobedience.

The thirty-second: Lack of contentment opens the gate of innovation (bid'a), and contentment closes that gate. If you reflect on the innovations of the Rāfiḍa, the Nawāṣib, and the Khawārij, you will see them arising from lack of contentment with the cosmic judgment (ḥukm kawnī), or the religious judgment (ḥukm dīnī), or both.

The thirty-third: Contentment is the axis of the order of religion, outward and inward. Matters do not fall outside five types. They are divided into two divisions: religious and cosmic. These are commanded things, forbidden things, permissible things, pleasant blessings, and painful afflictions.

When the servant applies contentment to all of this, he has taken the abundant share of Islam and won the highest arrow (qidḥ al-mu'allā).

The thirty-fourth: Contentment saves the servant from contesting the Lord, exalted is He, in His rulings and decrees. Discontent with Him is a form of contention with Him regarding what the servant has not been content with. The root of Iblis's contention with his Lord lies in his not being content with His decrees and rulings, both religious and cosmic. Had he been content, he would not have been transformed from the angelic reality to the satanic, Iblisian reality.

The thirty-fifth: Everything in existence has been brought into being by the will of God, His wisdom, and His dominion. It is the necessary consequence of His names and attributes. Whoever is not content with what his Lord is content with has not been content with His names and attributes, and so has not been content with Him as Lord.

The thirty-sixth: Every decree that the servant dislikes and that does not suit him is one of two things: either it is a punishment for a sin, in which case it is a medicine for a sickness, which, were it not for the Wise One's provision of the medicine, the sickness would have carried him to destruction; or it is a cause of a blessing that cannot be attained except through that disliked thing. The disliked thing comes to an end and vanishes, while the blessing that follows from it is lasting and does not end. When the servant witnesses these two matters, the door of contentment with his Lord opens for him in everything that He decrees and ordains for him.

The thirty-seventh: The judgment of the Lord, exalted is He, is executed upon His servant, and His decree is just concerning him, as in the hadith: "Your judgment is executed upon me, Your decree is just upon me." Whoever is not content with justice is among the people of injustice and tyranny.

His saying "Your decree is just upon me" encompasses the decree of the sin, the decree of its consequence, and its punishment, for both are from His decree, mighty and majestic. He is the most just of the just in His decree regarding the sin and in His decree regarding its punishment.

As for His justice in punishment, it is evident. As for His justice in decreeing the sin, it is because the sin is a punishment for the heart's heedlessness of its Lord and its turning away from Him. When the heart is heedless of its Lord and its Protector, and its sincerity diminishes, it deserves to be struck with this punishment, for the hearts of the heedless are the mine of sins, and punishments descend upon them from every direction. Otherwise, with complete sincerity, remembrance, and turning toward God, glorified and exalted is He, and His remembrance, the occurrence of sin becomes impossible, as He, exalted is He, said: "Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality; indeed, he was of Our chosen servants" (Q. Yūsuf 12:24).

If you say: His decree upon His servant, by his turning away from Him, forgetting Him, and not being sincere, is a punishment for what? I say: This is the nature of the self and its condition. He, glorified is He, when He does not desire good for His servant, leaves him between himself, his nature, and his desire. That requires the effect of the self: heedlessness, forgetfulness, lack of sincerity, and following desire. These causes require their effects of pains and the loss of good things and pleasures, just as all causes require their effects and consequences.

If you say: Why did He not create him in a different attribute?
I say: This is a corrupt question, and its meaning is: Why did He not create him as an angel rather than a human?

If you say: Why did He not give him the success by which he is delivered from the evil of his self and the darkness of his nature?
I say: The meaning of this question is: Why did He not make all His creation equal? And why did He create opposites and differences? This is among the most corrupt questions. The requirement of His wisdom, lordship, and dominion for creating that has already been explained.

The thirty-eighth: Lack of contentment is either because of the loss of what has missed him of what he loves and desires, or because of encountering what he dislikes and is angry at. When he is certain that what missed him would not have reached him, and what reached him would not have missed him, then there is no benefit in his anger after that, except the loss of what benefits him and the arrival of what harms him.

The thirty-ninth: Contentment is among the deeds of the heart, comparable to jihad among the deeds of the limbs. Each of them is the peak of the hump of faith. Abu al-Dardā' said: "The peak of the hump of faith is patience with the judgment and contentment with the decree."

The fortieth: The first disobedience by which God was disobeyed in this world arose only from lack of contentment. Iblis did not accept God's judgment that He had decreed in cosmic form, namely the preference and honoring of Adam, nor His religious judgment, namely His command to prostrate to Adam. And Adam was not content with what had been permitted to him of the Garden, until he added to it eating from the tree of the fever (shajarat al-ḥummā). Then the disobediences of his offspring followed from lack of patience and lack of contentment.

The forty-first: The content person stands with God's choice for him, turning away from his own choice for himself. This comes from the strength of his knowledge of his Lord, exalted is He, and his knowledge of himself.

Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, Sufyān al-Thawrī, and Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ once gathered. Al-Thawrī said: "I used to dislike sudden death before today, but today I wish I were dead."

Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ said to him: "Why?" He said: "Because of what I fear of trial (fitna)."

Yūsuf said: "But I do not dislike a long life."

Al-Thawrī said: "And why do you dislike death?"

He said: "Perhaps I may come upon a day in which I repent and do righteous deeds."

Wuhayb was asked: "What do you say?"

He said: "I do not choose anything. Whatever is dearer to me is whatever is dearer to God."

Al-Thawrī kissed him between his eyes and said: "Spiritual, by the Lord of the Ka'bah."

This is the state of a servant for whom the state of life and death are equal; he stands with God's choice for him in them. Wuhayb, may God have mercy on him, had a high station of contentment and other stations.

The forty-second: That one know that God's withholding from His believing, loving servant is a gift (ʿaṭā'), and His trial of him is well-being (ʿāfiya).

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: "His withholding is a gift. That is because He did not withhold out of stinginess or lack, but He looked to the good of His believing servant and withheld by choice and good consideration."

This is as he said. He, glorified is He, does not decree for His believing servant any decree except that it is good for him, whether it displeases him or pleases him. So His decree for His believing servant of withholding is a gift, though in the form of withholding; and a blessing, though in the form of an ordeal; and His trial is well-being, though in the form of an affliction. But because of the servant's ignorance and wrongdoing, he counts as gift, blessing, and well-being only what he enjoys in the immediate present and what suits his nature. Had he been granted a full share of knowledge, he would count withholding a blessing and affliction a mercy; he would take more pleasure in affliction than in well-being, and more pleasure in poverty than in wealth, and in a state of scarcity he would be more grateful than in a state of abundance.

This was the state of the early generations (al-salaf).

The rational, contented person is one who counts affliction as well-being, deprivation as a blessing, and poverty as wealth.

It was revealed to one of the prophets: "When you see poverty approaching, say: Welcome, the emblem of the righteous. And when you see wealth approaching, say: A sin whose punishment has been hastened."

The one who is content (al-radi) is he who counts the blessings of God upon him in what he dislikes as greater and more numerous than His blessings upon him in what he loves. As one of the gnostics ('arifin) said: "O son of Adam, God's blessing upon you in what you dislike is greater than His blessing upon you in what you love." God, Exalted, has said: ﴿But it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. Another of the gnostics said: "Be content with God in everything He does to you, for He has withheld from you only to give to you, has afflicted you only to grant you well-being, has made you ill only to heal you, and has caused you to die only to bring you to life. Beware lest you abandon contentment with Him for the blink of an eye, lest you fall from His sight."

The forty-third: that he knows that He, glory be to Him, is the First before all things, the Last after all things, the Manifest of all things, the Owner of all things, and He creates what He wills and chooses. The servant has no right to choose over Him, and no one has any choice alongside Him. He does not share His judgment with anyone. The servant was not a thing worth mentioning. It is He, glory be to Him, who chose his existence, and chose that he should be as He decreed and decreed for him: in well-being and affliction, wealth and poverty, honour and humiliation, distinction and obscurity. Just as He, glory be to Him, is alone in creating, He is alone in choosing and disposing, and the servant has no share of that at all, for the whole matter belongs to God. God, Exalted, has said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿You have no part in the affair﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 128]. When the servant is certain that the whole matter belongs to God, and he has no part of the matter, small or great, then after this he has no recourse except contentment with the places where decrees fall, and with what his Lord brings about by His choice.

The forty-fourth: God's contentment with the servant is greater than Paradise and all that is in it, because contentment is an attribute of God, and Paradise is His creation. God, Exalted, has said: ﴿And the pleasure of God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72], after His saying: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. But the pleasure of God is greater. That is the great achievement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]. This contentment is a recompense for their contentment with Him in this world, and since this recompense is the best of recompenses, its cause is the best of deeds.

The forty-fifth: when the servant is content with Him and with what He does in all states, he does not choose over Him in his requests. His contentment with what He allots to him, decrees for him and does to him makes him independent of that. He places his remembrance of Him in the place of his asking. Rather, his asking of Him becomes the help to remember Him and to attain His pleasure. Such a person is given the best that is given to any petitioner, as came in the hadith: "Whoever is occupied with My remembrance rather than asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask."

For those who ask have asked Him, and He has given them the bounty they asked for. And those who are content have been content with Him, and He has given them His contentment with them. Contentment does not prevent asking for the causes of contentment; rather, its people are insistent in asking Him for that.

The forty-sixth: the Prophet ﷺ used to urge toward the highest stations. If the servant is unable to reach them, he descends to the middle station, as he said: "Worship God as if you see Him." This is the station of watchfulness (muraqabah), which encompasses the stations of Islam, faith and excellence (ihsan). Then he said: "If you do not see Him, then He sees you." So he lowered him, when unable to attain the first station, to the second station, which is knowledge that God is aware of him, sees him, and witnesses His servant in public and in private. Likewise the other hadith: "If you are able to act for God with contentment together with certainty, then do so. If you are not able, then in patience upon what you dislike there is much good." Thus he raised him to the highest stations, then returned him to the middle of them if he could not reach the highest. The first is the station of excellence (ihsan), and the one to which he descends is the station of faith (iman). Beyond that there is nothing but the station of loss.

The forty-seventh: he ﷺ praised those who are content with the bitter decree, with judgment, knowledge, understanding, and nearness to the rank of prophethood, as in the hadith of the delegations who came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said: "What are you?" They said: "Believers." He said: "What is the sign of your faith?" They said: "Patience at affliction, gratitude in ease, and contentment with the bitter decree, truthfulness in the places of encounter, and abandoning gloating over enemies." He said: "You are wise scholars; you have nearly become prophets because of your understanding."

The forty-eighth: contentment holds the reins of all the stations of religion. It is their spirit and their life. It is the spirit of trust (tawakkul) and its reality, the spirit of certainty (yaqin), the spirit of love, the health of the lover, the proof of the sincerity of love, and the spirit and proof of gratitude.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "The sign of the love of God is abundant remembrance of Him, for you do not love anything without remembering it often. The sign of religion is sincerity to God in secret and in public. The sign of gratitude is contentment with God's decree and submission to His judgment."

Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari said: "I discussed with Abu Sulayman the report narrated: 'The first to be called to Paradise are the praisers (al-hammadun).' He said: 'Woe to you! It is not that you praise Him for a calamity while your heart is rebellious against you. If you are like that, return to the patient. Praise is only that you praise Him while your heart is submissive and content.'"

Thus contentment is like the spirit of these stations and the foundation upon which they are built. None of them is sound without it at all. And God knows best.

The forty-ninth: contentment takes the place of many acts of worship that burden the body, so his contentment becomes easier for him, sweeter for him, and raises his rank. It has been mentioned in an Israili report (athar isra'ili) that a worshipper worshipped God for a long time, and was shown in a dream that a certain shepherdess was his companion in Paradise. He asked about her until he found her. He lodged with her three nights to observe her deeds. He used to spend the night standing in prayer while she spent it sleeping, and he would fast while she would not fast. He said to her: "Do you have no deed other than what I have seen?" She said: "By God, that is all, or nothing but what you have seen. I know of no other." He kept saying to her: "Remember!" until she said: "There is one quality in me: If I am in hardship, I do not wish that I were at ease; if I am ill, I do not wish that I were healthy; if I am in the sun, I do not wish that I were in shade." He said: he placed his hand upon his head and said: "Is this a quality? By God, this is a great quality, which the worshippers cannot attain."

Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, related: "Whoever is content with what God sends down from the heaven to the earth, he is forgiven."

In a marfu' report (a report traced back to the Prophet ﷺ): "The best thing given to a servant is contentment with what God has apportioned to him."

In another report: "When God loves a servant He tests him. If he is patient, He chooses him. If he is content, He selects him."

In a report: The Children of Israel asked Moses to ask his Lord for something which, if they did it, He would be pleased with them. Moses said: "My Lord, You hear what they say." He said: "Tell them: They should be content with Me, until I am content with them."

In another report from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever wishes to know what he has with God, let him look at what God has with him, for God lowers the servant to the place where the servant himself lowers himself."

In another report: "Whoever is content with God for little provision, God is content with him for little deed."

One of the gnostics said: "I know of a world of the dead who look at their dwellings in the gardens from their graves; their provision from Paradise is brought to them morning and evening. Yet they are in grief and distress in the barzakh (the intermediate state). If it were divided among the people of a town, they would all die." It was said: "What were their deeds?" He said: "They were Muslims and believers, except that they had no share of trust or contentment."

In the counsel of Luqman to his son: "I counsel you with qualities that bring you near to God and keep you far from His anger: that you worship God and associate nothing with Him, and that you be content with God's decree regarding what you love and what you dislike."

One of the gnostics said: "Whoever trusts in God and is content with God's decree has established faith, has freed his hands and feet for seeking good, and has established the good characters that set his affairs right."

The fiftieth: contentment opens the door to good character with God, Exalted, and with people, for good character comes from contentment and bad character from discontent. Good character raises its possessor to the rank of one who fasts by day and prays by night, while bad character consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood.

The fifty-first: contentment produces the joy of the heart in what is decreed in all matters, good disposition and tranquility of the soul in every state, the calm of the heart at every frightening and distressing worldly matter, the coolness of contentment, the satisfaction of the servant with his portion from his Lord, his joy in his Master's care over him, his submission to his Master in everything, his acceptance of what He brings upon him, his surrender to Him in judgments and decrees, his belief in the goodness of His management and the perfection of His wisdom. It removes from him complaining to others about his Lord and resentment at His decrees. For this reason one of the gnostics called contentment "good character with God." It requires abandoning objection to Him in His dominion, and eliminating the useless speech that mars good character toward Him. So he does not say: "How much people need rain!" nor "This is a day of intense heat or intense cold," nor "Poverty is a trial, and dependants are worry and grief," and he does not name anything that God has decreed and ordained with a blameworthy name when God, glory be to Him and Exalted, has not blamed it. For all of this contradicts His contentment.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God have mercy on him, said: "I have awakened with no joy except in the places where decrees fall."

Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "Poverty and wealth are two riding beasts; I do not care which of them I mount. If it is poverty, in it is patience; if it is wealth, in it is giving."

Ibn Abi al-Hawari—or it was said to him—that so-and-so said: "I wish the night were longer than it is." He said: "He has done well and he has done ill. He did well in wishing its length for worship and intimate prayer, and he did ill in wishing for what God did not will and loving what God does not love."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "I do not care in what state I wake or evening comes, whether in hardship or ease."

One day he said to his wife 'Atikah, sister of Sa'id ibn Zayd, when he was angry with her: "By God, I will make you miserable!" She said: "Can you turn me away from Islam after God has guided me?" He said: "No." She said: "Then what can make me miserable?" She means that she was content with the places where decrees fall; nothing that befalls her from Him distresses her except being turned away from Islam, and he has no way to do that.

Al-Thawri said one day in the presence of Rabi'ah: "O God, be content with us." She said: "Are you not ashamed to ask Him for His contentment with you while you are not content with Him?" He said: "I ask God's forgiveness." Then Ja'far ibn Sulayman said to her: "When is the servant content with God?" She said: "When his joy in calamity is like his joy in blessing."

In a divine report: "What do My friends have to do with worldly concern? Worldly concern removes the sweetness of My intimate conversation from their hearts."

It was said: "Those most concerned with this world are those most concerned with the Hereafter, and those least concerned with this world are those least concerned with the Hereafter."

Thus faith in the decree and contentment with it removes from the servant worry, grief and sorrow.

A saint of God whose food came from garbage heaps was mentioned in the presence of Rabi'ah. A man present said: "What harm is there in this man asking God to make his provision from something other than this?" She said: "Be silent, you idler! Do you not know that the friends of God are more content with Him than to ask Him to move them to a livelihood, so that He may choose for them?"

In an Israili report: Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord what would bring His contentment. God revealed to him: "His contentment is in your dislike, but you cannot be patient with what you dislike." He said: "My Lord, guide me to it." He said: "His contentment is in your contentment with My decree."

In another narration: Musa (peace be upon him) said, "O Lord, which of Your creation is most beloved to You?" He said, "One whom, when I take from him what he loves, remains at peace with Me." He said, "Which of Your creation are You displeased with?" He said, "One who seeks My guidance (istikharah) in a matter, and when I decree it for him, he becomes angry at My decree."

In another narration: "I am Allah. There is no god but Me. I have measured the measures, arranged the arrangements, and perfected the making. Whoever is content, for him is My contentment until he meets Me. And whoever is discontent, for him is My discontent until he meets Me."

The fifty-second: The best of states is desire for Allah and what necessarily follows from it. This is not complete except through certainty (yaqin) and contentment with Allah. For this reason Sahl said: "People's share of certainty is in proportion to their share of contentment, and their share of contentment is in proportion to their desire for Allah."

The fifty-third: Contentment frees a person from blaming what Allah has not blamed and from disparaging what Allah has not disparaged. When a servant is not content with something, he finds faults in it in various ways and disparages it in various ways. This reflects a lack of modesty before Allah, a disparagement of what has committed no sin, and a fault-finding with His creation. This casts the servant down from the eyes of his Lord. If a man prepared food for you and presented it to you, and you found fault with it and disparaged it, you would be exposing yourself to his anger and contempt, and inviting him to cut that off from you. Some of the knowers of Allah (al-'arifin) have said: "Disparaging a made thing and finding fault with it, when its Maker has not disparaged it, is backbiting against it and a slight upon it."

The fifty-fourth: The Prophet (ﷺ) asked Allah for contentment with the decree, as in the Musnad and the Sunan: "O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, give me life if life is good for me, and take me if death is good for me. I ask You for fear of You in private and in public. I ask You for the word of truth in anger and in contentment. I ask You for moderation in poverty and wealth. I ask You for a bliss that does not end, and a coolness of the eye that does not cease. I ask You for contentment after the decree. I ask You for the coolness of life after death. I ask You for the delight of looking at Your noble Face, and for longing to meet You, without harm that injures, or a trial that misleads.
