Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 39, verse 33:

Those who bring the truth (al-ladhi ja'a bi-l-sidq): it is part of his character to be truthful in his speech, his action and his state. Truthfulness (al-sidq) lies in these three.

Truthfulness in statements is the straightness of the tongue upon sayings, like the straightness of the ear of grain upon its stalk.

Truthfulness in deeds is the straightness of actions upon the command and following (the Sunnah), like the straightness of the head upon the body.

Truthfulness in states is the straightness of the works of the heart and the limbs upon sincerity (ikhlas).

And exhausting one's capacity and expending one's effort: by this the servant becomes one of those who have brought the truth.

According to the perfection of these matters in him and his upholding of them, his siddiqiyyah (the state of being a siddiq) is determined.

For this reason Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him and content him, possessed the peak of the hump of siddiqiyyah, and he was called al-Siddiq without qualification.

Al-siddiq is more intensive than al-saddhuq (one who is very truthful), and al-saddhuq is more intensive than al-sadiq.

So the highest rank of truthfulness is the rank of siddiqiyyah.

It is the perfection of submission to the Messenger (ﷺ), together with the perfection of sincerity toward the One who sent him.

[Section: The Station of Discipline (manzilat al-riyada)]

Among the stations of "You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help" (﴿Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾) is the station of riyada (discipline, training).

It is the training of the soul in truthfulness and sincerity.

The author of al-Manazil (Abu Isma'il al-Ansari, Manazil al-sairin) said: it is the training of the soul to accept truthfulness.

This has two meanings: training it to accept truthfulness when it is presented to it in its sayings, actions and intentions; so when truthfulness is presented to it, it accepts it, submits to it and yields to it.

The second: accepting the truth from whoever presents it. Allah said: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the righteous﴾ [al-Zumar: 33].

Your own truthfulness is not sufficient; rather, you must be truthful and confirm the truthful. Many people are truthful, but pride or envy, or something else, prevents them from confirming (the truth).

He said: it has three degrees: general discipline, which is refining the morals through knowledge, purifying the deeds through sincerity, and fully observing the rights in dealings.

As for refining the morals through knowledge, it means reforming and purifying them according to the requirement of knowledge; so one does not move with any outward or inward movement except in accordance with knowledge, and thus outward and inward movements are weighed by the scale of the Sharia.

As for purifying deeds through sincerity, it is stripping them of any motive other than Allah; it is an expression for unifying the aim and stripping the motive toward Him.

As for fully observing rights in dealings, it is that you give what you have been commanded regarding the right of Allah and the rights of the servants completely and in full, having advised the rights-holder to the utmost degree of sincere counsel, and pleased him entirely, so that you gain his praise and gratitude.

And since these three are extremely burdensome upon the soul, their enforcement is called riyada; when one becomes accustomed to them, they become a character trait.

(Fā'ida)

His holding back of the soul for which death has been decreed does not preclude returning it to its dead body at some time, a temporary return that does not bring about the ordinary life of this world.

If the sleeper's soul is in his body while he is alive, and his life is not the life of one who is awake, then sleep is the sibling of death. Likewise, when the dead person's soul is returned to his body, his state is intermediate between the living and the dead whose souls have not returned to their bodies, like the state of the sleeper, which is intermediate between the living and the dead. Reflect on this, for it will clear away many difficulties for you.

[Section: Dreams]

What should be known is that what we have mentioned concerning the nature of the soul differs according to the condition of each soul in strength and weakness, greatness and smallness. The great, elevated soul has what the lesser one does not. You see how the rulings of souls in this world vary enormously, according to the separation of souls, their modes, their strengths, their slowness and swiftness, and what assists them. A soul freed from the captivity of the body, its attachments and its impediments, has a power, force, penetration, resolve, swiftness of ascent to God, and attachment to God that the soul humbled and imprisoned in the attachments and impediments of the body does not have. If this is so while it is confined in its body, how much more so when it is stripped bare, separated from the body, and its powers are gathered within it, and it was in its original nature a lofty, pure, great soul with lofty resolve. For such a soul there is, after separation from the body, a different condition and a different action.

Dreams have repeatedly shown, among all kinds of human beings, the actions of souls after their death, which they cannot perform while attached to the body: defeating great armies with one or two men or a small number, and the like. How often has the Prophet (ﷺ) been seen in a dream, with Abu Bakr and Umar, and their souls have routed the armies of unbelief and oppression, so that their armies are found defeated and broken despite their great numbers and equipment, and the weakness of the believers and their being killed.

Among the wonders is that the souls of believers who love one another and know one another meet even when the distance between them is greatest and most remote. They become familiar and acquainted, so that one recognizes the other as if he were his companion and associate. When he sees him, that matches what his soul had recognized before seeing him.

(Qāla) Abdullah ibn Amr said: "The souls of believers meet at a distance of one day's journey, though neither has ever seen the other." Some have traced this back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

(Wa-qāla) Ikrima and Mujahid said: "When a person sleeps, he has a conduit through which the soul flows, and its root is in the body. It reaches wherever God wills as long as it is going. The person is asleep; when it returns to the body, the person awakens. It is like the ray of the sun that falls on the earth, whose root remains connected to the sun."

Abu Abdullah ibn Mandah mentioned from some scholars that he said: "The soul extends from the nostril of a person, and its vehicle and its root are in his body. If the soul separated completely, he would die, just as if a lamp were separated from its wick. Do you not see that the vehicle of the fire is in the wick, and its light and radiance fill the house? Likewise, the soul extends from the person's nostril in his sleep, until it reaches the sky, roams the lands, and meets the souls of the dead. When the angel charged with the souls of servants shows him what he wishes to show him, and the one seen was intelligent, sharp-minded, truthful, and in his waking state did not turn to anything false, his soul returns to him and conveys to his heart the truth of what God the Mighty and Majestic showed him, according to his nature. But if he was dull, reckless, and loved falsehood and looking at it, then when he sleeps and God shows him something good or evil, his soul returns to him, and wherever it sees some of the Devil's trickery or falsehood, it stops there as it does in waking. Thus it does not convey it to his heart, and he does not comprehend what he saw, because he mixed truth with falsehood. An interpreter cannot interpret for him, since he has mixed truth with falsehood."

This is among the best of statements, and it is evidence of its speaker's knowledge and insight into souls and their rulings.

You see a man hear knowledge and wisdom, which are the most beneficial things for him, then pass by falsehood, frivolity, singing, doubt, lies, or other things, and he attends to them and opens his heart to them until they reach it. The knowledge and wisdom he heard become confused in him, and truth becomes mixed with falsehood for him. So it is with the souls during sleep. As for after separation, they are tormented by those beliefs and false doubts that were their portion while attached to the body, and added to that is their torment by those desires and appetites from which they were barred, and added to that is another torment that God produces for them and for their body from the deeds in which they shared with it. This is the "constricted life" in the barzakh and the provision with which they equip themselves for it.

But the pure, lofty, true soul, which does not love falsehood or become familiar with it, is in contrast to all of that: it delights in those sound beliefs, sciences, and cognitions that it received from prophethood, and in those pure aspirations and resolves. God the Glorified produces for it from its deeds a bliss with which He blesses it in the barzakh, so that it becomes for it a garden among the gardens of Paradise, while for the other there is a pit among the pits of Hellfire.

[Question: Do the souls of the living and the souls of the dead meet or not?]

The evidences for this question are more than anyone can count except God Most High, and sense perception and experience are among the most just witnesses to it. The souls of the living and the dead meet just as the souls of the living meet. God Most High has said: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep. Then He withholds those on which He has decreed death and sends the others back until a specified term. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾

(Qāla) Abu Abdullah ibn Mandah: "Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim told us; Abdullah ibn Husayn al-Harrani told us, and my grandfather Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb told us: Musa ibn A'yan told us, from Mutarrif, from Ja'far Abi al-Mughira, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding this verse, that he said: 'It has reached me that the souls of the living and the dead meet in sleep, and they ask one another, and God withholds the souls of the dead and sends the souls of the living back to their bodies.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim said in his Tafsir: "Abdullah ibn Sulayman told us; al-Husayn told us; Amir told us; Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying {and those that have not died during their sleep}: He takes it in its sleep, so the soul of the living and the soul of the dead meet, and they discuss and recognize one another. Then the soul of the living returns to its body in the world to the remainder of its term, while the soul of the dead wishes to return to its body but is held back."

This is one of two views on the verse: that the one withheld is the one whose death was its first taking, and the one sent back is the one taken in sleep. According to this view, the meaning is that the soul of the dead person is taken, and He withholds it and does not send it back to its body before the Day of Resurrection, and the soul of the sleeper is taken, then He sends it back to its body for the remainder of its term, and then it is taken by the other taking.

The second view on the verse is that both the withheld and the sent-back souls are taken by the taking of sleep. Whoever has completed its term, He withholds it with Himself and does not send it back to its body; whoever has not completed its term, He sends it back to its body so that it may complete its term. Shaykh al-Islam chose this view and said: "The Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate it." He said: "God mentioned the withholding of those souls on which death was decreed from among those souls that He took in sleep. As for those He took at the time of their death, He did not describe them by withholding or sending back; they are a third category."

What is preponderant is the first view, because God informed of two takings: a greater taking, which is the taking of death, and a lesser taking, which is the taking of sleep. He divided the souls into two categories: one for which He decreed death and withheld it with Himself, which is the one He took by the taking of death; and one for which a remainder of term was decreed, and He sent it back to its body until it completed its term. God made withholding and sending back the rulings for the two takings mentioned first: this one is withheld, and that one is sent back. He informed that the one that did not die is the one taken in its sleep. Had He divided the taking of sleep into two categories, a taking of death and a taking of sleep, He would not have said {and those that have not died during their sleep}, for from the moment it was seized it died, and He has informed that it did not die. How then could He say afterward {then He withholds those on which He has decreed death}?

For one who perceives this view, one might say that His saying {then He withholds those on which He has decreed death} comes after He took it by the taking of sleep: He took it first by the taking of sleep, then decreed death upon it afterward. The truth is that the verse encompasses both types, for He mentioned two takings, the taking of sleep and the taking of death, and He mentioned the withholding of the one taken and the sending back of the other. It is known that He withholds the soul of every dead person, whether it died in sleep or in waking, and He sends back the soul of one who has not died. So His saying {God takes the souls at the time of their death} encompasses the one who died in waking and the one who died in sleep.

The meeting of the souls of the living and the dead is also indicated by the fact that the living person sees the dead in his dream, asks him, and the dead informs him of what the living does not know, and his report coincides with what he said regarding the past and the future. Sometimes he informs him of money the dead buried in a place known to no one else, and sometimes of a debt upon him, mentioning its evidence and proofs.

More striking than this, he informs him of what he did of deeds that no one among the worlds had witnessed, and more striking still, he tells him, "You will come to us at such and such a time," and it happens as he said. Sometimes he informs him of matters that the living is certain no one else knew. We have mentioned the story of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama and what he said to Awf ibn Malik, and we have mentioned the story of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas and his informing one who saw him that he had a debt that was owed.

And the story of Sadaqa ibn Sulayman al-Ja'fari and his son's informing him of what was done after him.

And the story of Shabib ibn Shayba, and his mother's words to him after death: "May God reward you with good for having taught her, 'There is no god but God.'"

And the story of al-Fadl ibn al-Muwaffaq with his son, and his informing him of his knowledge of his visit.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "Abdullah ibn Salam and Salman al-Farisi met, and one said to the other: 'If I die before you, meet me and inform me what you encountered from your Lord, and if I die before you, I will meet you and inform you.' The other said: 'Do the dead and the living meet?' He said: 'Yes, their souls are in Paradise and go wherever they wish.' He said: 'So-and-so died, and he met him in a dream and said: "Put your trust and rejoice. I have never seen anything like trust."'"

Al-Amir ibn Abd al-Muttalib said: "I used to long to see Umar in a dream, and I did not see him until the year was near its end. I saw him wiping sweat from his forehead, saying: 'This is the time of my leisure. My throne almost collapsed, had I not met the Compassionate, the Merciful.'"

When death came to Shurayh ibn Abid al-Thumali, Ghudayf ibn al-Harith entered upon him while he was struggling with his soul, and said: "O Abu al-Hajjaj, if you are able to come to us after death and tell us what you see, then do so." He said: and he was a word accepted among the people of jurisprudence. He said: "He remained a while without seeing him, then he saw him in a dream and said to him: 'Have you not died?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'How is your state?' He said: 'Our Lord forgave the sins, and none of us was destroyed except the cripples.' I said: 'And what are the cripples?' He said: 'Those who are pointed at with fingers over something.'"

Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: "I saw my father in a dream after his death, as if he were in a garden. He handed me some apples, and I interpreted them as children. I said: 'Which of the deeds did you find best?' He said: 'Seeking forgiveness, my son.'"

Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik saw Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz after his death and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I wish I knew what state you have come to after death." He said: "O Maslama, this is the time of my leisure. By God, I have not rested except now." I said: "Where are you, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "With the imams of guidance in the Garden of Eden."

Salih al-Barrad said: "I saw Zurara ibn Awfa after his death and said: 'May God have mercy on you, what was said to you and what did you say?'" He turned away from me. I said: "What did God do with you?" He said: "He showed favor to me by His generosity and nobility." I said: "What about Abu al-Ala ibn Yazid, the brother of Mutarrif?" He said: "He is in the high ranks." I said: "Which deeds are most effective in what you have?" He said: "Trust in God and shortening hope."

Malik ibn Dinar said: "I saw Muslim ibn Yasar after his death, and I greeted him, but he did not return my greeting. I said: 'What prevents you from returning the greeting?' He said: 'I am dead, so how can I return your greeting?' I said to him: 'What did you encounter after death?' He said: 'By God, I encountered terrors and great, severe tremors.' I said: 'And what came after that?' He said: 'And what do you think would come from the Generous? He accepted our good deeds, pardoned us for our misdeeds, and took on our burdens for us.'" He said: Malik then let out a sob and fell unconscious. He said: He remained sick for some days after that, then his heart burst and he died.

Suhayl, the brother of Hazm, said: "I saw Malik ibn Dinar after his death, and I said: 'O Abu Yahya, I wish I knew what you brought before God.' He said: 'I brought many sins, which He erased for me, and good opinion of God the Mighty and Majestic.'"

When Rija' ibn Hayat died, a pious woman saw him and said: "O Abu al-Miqdam, to what have you come?" He said: "To good. But we were startled after you by a startle, and we thought the Resurrection had come." She said: "I said: 'And why is that?'" He said: "Al-Jarrah and his companions entered Paradise with their burdens, until they crowded at its gate."

Jamil ibn Murra said: "Muwarriq al-Ijli was a brother and friend to me, and I said to him one day: 'Whichever of us dies before the other, let him come to his companion and inform him of what he has come to.'" He said: "Muwarriq died, and my family saw him in a dream as if he came to us as he used to come, and knocked on the door as he used to knock. She said: 'I got up and opened to him as I used to open, and I said: "Enter, O Abu al-Mu'tamir, to your brother's door."' He said: 'How can I enter when I have tasted death? I came only to inform Jamil of what God has done with me. Tell him that He has made me among the near ones.'"

When Muhammad ibn Sirin died, some of his companions grieved for him intensely. He saw him in a dream in a good state and said: "O my brother, I see you in a state that pleases me. What did al-Hasan do?" He said: "He was raised above me by seventy degrees." I said: "And why is that, when we used to think you were better than him?" He said: "That is because of his long grief."

Ibn Uyayna said: "I saw Sufyan al-Thawri in a dream and said: 'Advise me.' He said: 'Reduce your acquaintance with people.'"

Ammar ibn Sayf said: "I saw al-Hasan ibn Salih in my dream and said: 'I have been longing to meet you. What do you have, so that you may tell us?' He said: 'Rejoice, for I have not seen anything like good opinion of God.'"

When Daygham the worshipper died, one of his companions saw him in a dream and said: "Did you not pray over me?" He said: he mentioned an illness that he had, and he said: "If you had prayed over me, you would have gained your head."

When Rabi'a died, a woman of her companions saw her wearing a garment of brocade and a veil of silk, though she had been shrouded in a woolen robe and veil. She said to her: "What became of the robe in which you were shrouded, and the woolen veil?" She said: "By God, it was removed from me and replaced with this which you see on me. My shrouds were folded and sealed, and they were raised to 'Illiyyin, so that their reward may be completed for me on the Day of Resurrection." She said: "I said to her: 'Is this what you used to work for in the days of the world?'" She said: "And what is this compared to what I have seen of God's honor for His friends?"

I said to her: "What became of Abida bint Abi Kilab?" She said: "Far away! By God, she outstripped us to the high ranks." She said: "I said: 'And why, when she was more worshipful than her among the people?'" She said: "She never cared in what state she woke or evening came upon her in the world."

I said: "What became of Abu Malik (meaning Daygham)?" She said: "He visits God, Blessed and Most High, whenever he wishes."

She said: "I said: 'What became of Bishr ibn Mansur?'" She said: "Bravo, bravo! By God, he was given beyond what he hoped."

She said: "I said: 'Advise me with a matter by which I may draw near to God, Most High.'" She said: "Be constant in the remembrance of God, for you will soon be envied for it in your grave."

When Abd al-Aziz ibn Sulayman the worshipper died, one of his companions saw him wearing green garments, with a crown of pearls on his head. He said: "How were you after us, and how did you find the taste of death, and how did you see the matter there?" He said: "As for death, do not ask about its severe distress and grief, except that the mercy of God inherits every defect from us, and we met nothing except by His bounty."

Salih ibn Bishr said: "When Ata al-Sulami died, I saw him in my dream and said: 'O Abu Muhammad, are you not among the group of the dead?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Where have you gone after death?' He said: 'By God, I have gone to much good and a Lord who is forgiving and grateful.' I said: 'By God, you used to have long sorrow in the abode of the world.' He smiled and said: 'By God, that has brought me a long rest and lasting joy.' I said: 'In which of the ranks are you?' He said: ﴿With those whom God has blessed of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. And excellent are those as companions.﴾"

(And when he died) — ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī — one of his relatives saw him in a dream and said: "Have you not died?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then where are you?" He said: "By Allah, I am in a garden of the gardens of Paradise, I and a group of my companions. We gather every Friday night and the morning after it at Bakr ibn ʿAbdullah al-Muzanī, and we receive your news." He said: I asked: "Are your bodies or your spirits?" He said: "Far from it! The bodies have decayed; only the spirits meet."

(And he was seen) — al-Faḍl ibn ʿIyāḍ — after his death, and he said: "I have not seen anything better for the servant than his Lord."

(And Murrah al-Hamdānī) had prostrated so much that the dust had eaten his forehead. When he died, a man of his family saw him in his dream, and the place of his prostration was like a shining star. He said: "What is this mark I see on your face?" He said: "The place of prostration was clothed with light by the dust that ate it." I said: "What is your station in the Hereafter?" He said: "The best abode: a house whose people do not move from it, and they do not die."

(And) Abū Yaʿqūb al-Qāriʾ said: I saw in my dream a tall, wheat-complexioned man, and people were following him. I said: "Who is this?" They said: "Uways al-Qaranī." So I followed him and said: "Advise me, may Allah have mercy on you." He frowned in my face. I said: "A seeker seeking guidance; guide me, may Allah have mercy on you." So he turned to me and said: "Seek the mercy of Allah in His love (for you); beware His vengeance at the time of your disobedience; and do not cut off your hope in Him in between those two." Then he turned away and left me.

(And) Ibn al-Simāk said: I saw Mis'ar in a dream and I said: "Which deeds did you find best?" He said: "Gatherings of remembrance."

(And al-Ajlaḥ said:) I saw Salamah ibn Kuhayl in a dream and I said: "Which deeds did you find best?" He said: "Standing in prayer at night."

(And) Abū Bakr ibn Abī Maryam said: I saw Wafāʾ ibn Bishr after his death and I said: "What became of you, O Wafāʾ?" He said: "I was saved after every hardship." I said: "Which deeds did you find best?" He said: "Weeping out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

(And) al-Layth ibn Saʿd said, from Mūsā ibn Wardān, that he saw ʿAbdullah ibn Abī Ḥabībah after his death, and he said: "My good deeds were presented to me and my bad deeds. I saw among my good deeds pomegranate seeds, which I picked up and ate, and I saw among my bad deeds two silk threads that were in my cap."

(And) Saʿīd ibn Dāwūd said: My brother Ibn Dāwūd narrated to me, from Juwayriyah ibn Asmāʾ, who said: "We were in ʿAbbādān when a worshipful young man from the people of Kufa came to us, and he died there on a day of intense heat. I said: 'Let us cool down, then we will prepare his burial,' and I slept. I saw as if I were in the graveyard, and suddenly there was a remaining jewel shining in beauty, and I was looking at it. A maiden appeared from it, whose beauty I had never seen the like of. She came to me and said: 'By Allah, do not hold him back from us until midday.' So I woke up in alarm, took up his preparation, and dug him a grave in the place where I had seen the dome, and I buried him there."

And ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAttāb al-Laythī said: I saw ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays in a dream and I said: "Which deeds did you find best?" He said: "That which is done seeking the Face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

And Yazīd ibn Hārūn said: I saw Abū al-ʿAlāʾ Ayyūb ibn Abī Miskīn in a dream and I said: "What did your Lord do with you?" He said: "He forgave me." I said: "For what?" He said: "For fasting and prayer." I said: "Have you seen Manṣūr ibn Zādhān?" He said: "Far from it! We see his palace from afar."

And Yazīd ibn Nuʿāmah said: A girl died in the plague of al-Jārif, and her father met her after her death and said to her: "O my daughter, tell me about the Hereafter." She said: "O father, we have come upon a great matter: you know but do not act, and you know and do not act. By Allah, one tasbīḥah or two tasbīḥahs, or one rakʿah or two rakʿahs, in the record of my deeds, are dearer to me than the world and what is in it."

And Kathīr ibn Murrah said: I saw in my dream as if I had entered a lofty degree in Paradise, and I began to walk around it and grew weary of it. Then suddenly I saw women from among the women of the mosque in one part of it. I went until I greeted them, then I said: "By what did you reach this degree?" They said: "By prostrations and takbīrs."

And Mizāḥim, the freedman of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, narrated from Fāṭimah bint ʿAbd al-Malik, the wife of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz woke up one night and said: "I have seen a wondrous vision!"
She said: I said: "May I be your ransom, tell me of it?" He said: "I will not tell you until morning." When dawn broke, he went out, prayed, then returned to his place of sitting. She said: I seized his privacy and said: "Tell me of the vision you saw." He said: "I saw as if I had been raised to a wide green land, as if it were a green carpet, and in it was a white palace like silver. Suddenly, someone came out of that palace and called out with his loudest voice: 'Where is Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib? Where is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and entered the palace. Then another came out of that palace and called: 'Where is Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, the son of Abū Quḥāfah?' Abū Bakr came and entered that palace. Then another came out and called: 'Where is ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb?' ʿUmar came and entered that palace. Then another came out and called: 'Where is ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān?' He came and entered that palace. Then another came out and called: 'Where is ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib?' He came and entered that palace. Then another came out and called: 'Where is ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz?'" ʿUmar said: "I stood up until I entered that palace. I was pushed toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with the people around him. I said to myself: 'Where should I sit?' So I sat beside ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. I looked, and Abū Bakr was on the right of the Prophet ﷺ, and ʿUmar was on his left. I looked carefully, and between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abū Bakr there was a man. I said: 'Who is this man between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abū Bakr?' He said: 'This is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam.' Then I heard a caller calling, with a veil between me and him: 'Be illuminated, O ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz! Hold fast to what you are upon, and remain steadfast upon what you are upon.' Then it was as if he gave me permission to leave, and I left that palace. I turned behind me and saw ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān coming out of that palace saying: 'Praise be to Allah who has given me victory,' and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in a circle outside that palace, saying: 'Praise be to Allah who has forgiven me.'"

(And) Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah narrated from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Abū Bakr and ʿUmar were sitting with him. I greeted and sat down. While I was sitting, ʿAlī and Muʿāwiyah were brought in, and they were placed in a room, and the door was closed on them while I was watching. Hardly had ʿAlī come out, saying: 'It has been decided in my favour, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah!' and hardly had Muʿāwiyah come out after him, saying: 'I have been forgiven, by the Lord of the Kaʿbah!'"

(And) Ḥammād ibn Abī Hāshim said: A man came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a dream, with Abū Bakr on his right and ʿUmar on his left, and two men came approaching, disputing, while you were sitting before him. He said to you: 'O ʿUmar, when you act, act with the deed of these two, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.'" ʿUmar made him swear by Allah: "Did you really see this dream?" He swore, and ʿUmar wept.

(And) ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm said: I saw Muʿādh ibn Jabal three days after his death, on a piebald horse, and behind him were white men wearing green garments, on piebald horses, and he was in front of them, saying: "﴿Would that my people knew what my Lord has forgiven me and made me of the honoured.﴾" Then he turned to his right and left, saying: "O Ibn Rawāḥah! O Ibn Maẓʿūn! ﴿All praise is for Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth, to dwell in Paradise wherever we wish; how excellent is the reward of the workers.﴾" Then he shook my hand and greeted me.

(And) Qabīṣah ibn ʿUqbah said: I saw Sufyān al-Thawrī in a dream after his death, and I said: "What did Allah do with you?" He said:
"I looked at my Lord face to face, and He said to me: 'Congratulations, Our pleasure is upon you, O son of Saʿīd.'
For you were one who stood much in prayer when the night grew dark, with the grief of the sorrowful and a heart full of longing.
So take for yourself whichever palace you wish, and visit Me, for I am not far from you."

And Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said: I saw Sufyān al-Thawrī after his death, flying in Paradise from a palm tree to a tree, and from a tree to a palm tree, saying: "﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾" It was said to him: "By what did you enter Paradise?" He said: "By scrupulousness, by scrupulousness." It was said to him: "What became of ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim?" He said: "We see him only like a star."

(And) Shuʿbah ibn al-Ḥajjāj and Mis'ar ibn Kidām were memorizers of ḥadīth and they were eminent. Abū Aḥmad al-Buraydī said: "I saw them after their death, and I said: 'O Abā Bisṭām, what did Allah do with you?'" He said:
"May Allah grant you success in memorizing what I say:
My God gave me in Paradise a remnant, which has a thousand doors of silver and jewels.
And the Merciful said to me: 'O Shuʿbah, you who delved deep into the gathering of knowledge and increased it:
Enjoy closeness to Me, for I am pleased with you, and with My servant Mis'ar, who stood in prayer at night.
Mis'ar, the one who was honoured with the promise that he would visit Me, and I would unveil My noble face for him to look upon.
This is My treatment of those who worshipped and did not become acquainted, in bygone ages, with what was disapproved.'"

Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Labdī said: I saw Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal in a dream and said: "O Abā ʿAbdillāh, what did Allah do with you?" He said: "He forgave me." He said: "O Aḥmad, did you strike sixty lashes for Me?" I said: "Yes, O Lord." He said: "This is My Face; I have permitted you; look at it."

And Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥajjāj said: A man of the people of Ṭarṭūs narrated to me, saying: "I asked Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to show me the people of the graves so that I could ask them about Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, what Allah did with him. After ten years, I saw in a dream as if the people of the graves had risen from their graves, and they hastened to speak to me, saying: 'O man, how long will you ask Allah to show you us, to ask us about a man who, since he parted from you, has not ceased to be adorned by the angels beneath the tree of Ṭūbā.'" Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq said: This speech from the people of the graves is only an informing of the high rank of Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, the elevation of his place, and the greatness of his station; they could not describe the nature of his state, or what he is in, except by this and what is similar to it.

And Abū Jaʿfar al-Saqqāʾ, companion of Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith, said: I saw Bishr al-Ḥāfī and Maʿrūf al-Karkhī, and they were coming, and I said: "From where?" They said: "From the Paradise of Firdaws; we visited the Interlocutor of Allah, Mūsā."

And ʿĀṣim al-Jazarī said: I saw in a dream as if I met Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith, and I said: "From where, O Abā Naṣr?" He said: "From ʿIlliyyīn." I said: "What did Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal do?" He said: "I left him just now with ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Warrāq before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the two of them eating and drinking." I said to him: "And you?" He said: "He knew my little desire for food, so He permitted me to look at Him."

And Abū Jaʿfar al-Saqqāʾ said: I saw Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith in a dream after his death, and I said: "O Abā Naṣr, what did Allah do with you?" He said: "He showed kindness to me and had mercy on me, and He said to me: 'O Bishr, even if you had prostrated to Me in the world on embers, you would not have rendered the thanks due for what I have filled the hearts of My servants with from you.' He permitted me half of Paradise, so I roam in it wherever I wish, and He promised that He would forgive whoever follows my funeral procession." I said: "What became of Abū Naṣr al-Tammār?" He said: "He is above people in his patience with his trials and his poverty."

Abd al-Ḥaqq said: Perhaps he meant by his words "half of Paradise," half of its bliss, because its bliss is of two halves: a spiritual half and a physical half. They enjoy first the spiritual, and when the spirits are returned to the bodies, the physical bliss is added to the spiritual. Others said: the bliss of Paradise is arranged according to knowledge and deed, and Bishr's share of deed was fuller than his share of knowledge. And Allah knows best.

And some of the righteous said: I saw Abū Bakr al-Shiblī in a dream, as if he were sitting in the gathering of al-Ruṣāfah, in the place where he used to sit. Suddenly he came, wearing fine garments. I stood up to him, greeted him, and sat before him. I said: "Who is the closest of your companions to you?" He said: "The most of them in remembrance of Allah, the most upright of them in the right of Allah, and the swiftest of them in hastening to seek Allah's pleasure."

And Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sāḥilī said: I saw Maysarah ibn Sulaym in a dream after his death, and I said to him: "Your absence has been long!" He said: "The long journey." I said: "And what did you come before Him with?" He said: "I was given a concession, because we used to issue fatwās with concessions." I said: "What do you command me?" He said: "Following the narrations, and keeping company with the righteous; these two save from the Fire and bring one near to the Almighty."

And Abū Jaʿfar al-Ḍarīr said: I saw ʿĪsā ibn Zādhān after his death, and I said: "What did Allah do with you?" He began to recite:
"If you saw the beautiful maidens of Paradise around me, and the flagons with them for drink,
Singing together with the Book, walking about in trailing garments."

And one of the companions of Ibn Jurayj said: I saw in a dream as if I came to the graveyard that is in Makkah, and I saw over its people a canopy, and I saw among them a grave over which was a canopy, a tent, and a lote tree. I came until I entered, and I greeted it, and there was Muslim ibn al-Rinjī. I greeted him and said: "O Abā Khālid, what is the matter with these graves having canopies, and your grave has a canopy and a tent and a lote tree in it?" He said: "I used to fast much." I said: "Then where is the grave of Ibn Jurayj and where is his place? For I used to sit with him and I wish to greet him." He said: "Like this," and with his hand, "far from it," and he turned his index finger, "and as for the grave of Ibn Jurayj, his record was raised in ʿIlliyyīn."

Ḥammād ibn Salamah saw his companions in a dream and said to them: "What did Allah do with you?" They said: "He said to me: 'You strained yourself much in the world, so today I will lengthen your rest and the rest of those who toiled.'"

This is a very long chapter. If your soul does not allow you to accept it and you say: "These are dreams, and they are not infallible," then consider one who sees a companion or a relative or someone else, and is informed of a matter that only the owner of the dream knows; or is told of money he buried; or is warned of a matter that will occur; or is given glad tidings of a matter that will be found, and it happens as he said; or he is told that he or some of his family will die by such-and-such a time, and it happens as he was told; or he is informed of abundance or drought, an enemy, a calamity, an illness, or a need of his, and it happens as he was informed. The number of what occurs of this kind none can count but Allah, and people share in it. We and others have seen wondrous things of this kind.

And refuted is the one who says that all of these are knowledge and beliefs within the soul that appear to its owner when the soul is released from bodily preoccupations by sleep. This is falsehood and impossibility, for the soul never had knowledge of these matters that the dead one reports, nor did they occur to its mind, nor was there any sign or indication of them in any way. We do not deny that the matter may happen in this way.

Indeed, among dreams are those that arise from the self's discourse and the form of belief; in fact, many of people's visions are merely forms of their beliefs, whether they correspond or do not correspond.

For dreams are of three kinds: a dream from Allah, a dream from Satan, and a dream from the self's discourse.

True dreams have divisions: among them is an inspiration that Allah, glory be to Him, casts into the heart of the servant, which is a speech the Lord addresses to His servant in sleep, as ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit and others said.

Among them is a likeness that the angel of dreams, who is charged with them, presents to him.

Among them is the meeting of the sleeper's spirit with the spirits of the dead from his family, relatives, companions and others, as we have mentioned.

Among them is the ascent of his spirit to Allah, glory be to Him, and its address to Him.

Among them is his spirit's entry into Paradise and its witnessing of it, and other things. So the meeting of the spirits of the living and the dead is one kind of true dream, which people regard as of the same kind as sensible things.

He, may He be blessed and exalted, informed that intercession belongs to the One who possesses the heavens and the earth, and He alone is God.

He is the One who intercedes through Himself to Himself, out of His mercy toward His servant. He then permits whomever He wills to intercede for someone.

So in reality, intercession belongs to Him. The one who intercedes before Him does so only by His permission and command, after His own intercession to Himself, which is His will to have mercy on His servant.

This is the opposite of the polytheistic intercession (al-shafa'a al-shirkiyya, intercession that associates partners with God) that these polytheists affirmed, and those who agreed with them. God nullified it in His Book with His words:

﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another at all, nor will any ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:123). And His words:

﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you before there comes a day in which there is no trade, no friendship, and no intercession﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:254). And He said:

﴿And warn with it those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord, having besides Him no protector and no intercessor, that they may become righteous﴾ (al-An'am 6:51). And He said:

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself above the Throne. You have not besides Him any protector or intercessor﴾ (al-Sajdah 32:4).

So He informed that the servants have no intercessor besides Him. Rather, when God wills mercy for His servant, He permits whomever He wills to intercede for him, as He said:

﴿There is no intercessor except after His permission﴾ (Yunus 10:3). And He said:

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:255). So intercession by His permission is not intercession besides Him, and the intercessor is not an intercessor besides Him; rather, he is an intercessor by His permission.

The difference between the two intercessors is like the difference between a partner and a commanded servant.

The intercession that God nullified is the intercession of a partner, for He has no partner. The intercession that He affirmed is that of a commanded servant, who does not intercede or advance before his master until he is permitted, and the master says: "Intercede for so-and-so." For this reason, the people most fortunate with His intercession on the Day of Resurrection, the lord of intercessors, are the people of tawhid (monotheism), who purified tawhid and cleansed it of the attachments and taints of shirk. They are those with whom God is pleased.

He said:

﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:28). And He said:

﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose word He has approved﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:109).

So He informed that on that day no effective intercession will occur except after the approval of the speech of the one for whom intercession is made, and His permission for the intercessor. As for the polytheist, He does not approve of him, nor is his word approved, so He does not permit the intercessors to intercede for him. He has linked intercession to two matters: His approval of the one for whom intercession is made, and His permission for the intercessor. As long as the two matters together are not present, intercession does not occur.

The secret of this is that to God alone belongs the entire command, so no one shares anything of the command with Him. The highest, most excellent, and most honored of creation before Him are the messengers and the near angels, and they are pure servants. They do not precede Him in speech, do not advance before Him, and do not act except after His permission and command. Especially on a day when no soul can avail another at all, they are owned and sustained, and their actions are bound by His command and permission. When the polytheist associates them with God and takes them as intercessors besides Him, thinking that if he does so they will advance and intercede for him with God, he is among the most ignorant of people regarding the right of the Lord, what is due to Him, and what is impossible for Him. This is an impossible and forbidden thing, resembling the analogy of the Exalted Lord with kings and great men, where a man takes one of their intimates and allies to intercede for him with them regarding his needs.

By this corrupt analogy, idols were worshipped, and the polytheists took intercessors and protectors besides God.

The difference between them is the difference between the created and the Creator, the lord and the sustained, the master and the servant, the owner and the owned, the wealthy and the poor, the one who has no need of anyone at all, and the one who is in every way in need of another.

The intercessors of created beings are their partners, for the settlement of their affairs depends on them. They are their helpers and supporters, and the authority of kings and great men stands by them. Without them, their hands and tongues would not extend among the people. Because of their need for them, kings must accept their intercession, even if they did not permit it or approve of the intercessor, for they fear that if they reject it, their obedience will break and those helpers will go to others. So they have no choice but to accept their intercession, willingly or unwillingly.

As for the Rich, whose richness is a necessary attribute of His essence, everything other than Him is poor in its essence. Everyone in the heavens and the earth is a servant of Him, subdued by His domination, and turned about by His will. If He destroyed them all, it would not diminish His might, His sovereignty, His dominion, His lordship, or His divinity by the weight of an atom.

He said:

﴿Those who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary," have certainly disbelieved. Say: "Then who could prevent Allah at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and everyone on the earth entirely?" And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. He creates what He wills, and Allah is over all things competent﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:17).

Concerning the chief of the verses of the Qur'an, the Verse of the Throne (ayat al-kursi), He said:

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:255). And He said:

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs all intercession. To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth"﴾ (al-Zumar 39:44).

So He informed that the state of His possession of the heavens and the earth necessitates that all intercession belongs to Him alone, and that no one intercedes with Him except by His permission. He is not a partner, but a pure possession, unlike the intercession of worldly people for one another.

It becomes clear that the intercession which God, may He be exalted, denied in the Qur'an is this polytheistic intercession that people know and some practice with one another. For this reason, its denial is sometimes stated absolutely, on the basis that it is the familiar intercession commonly relied upon among people. And sometimes it is restricted by saying that it benefits only after His permission. This intercession, in reality, comes from Him, for He is the One who permits it, the One who accepts it, and the One who is pleased with the one for whom intercession is made, and the One who enabled him to do what makes him deserving of intercession and of his speech.

So the one who takes an intercessor is a polytheist, whose intercession does not benefit him and who will not be interceded for. But the one who takes the Lord alone as his god, worshipped, beloved, hoped in, and feared, the one who draws near to Him alone, seeks His hope, and keeps far from His wrath, is the one for whom God, may He be exalted, permits the intercessor to intercede.

He, the Exalted, said:

﴿Or have they taken intercessors besides Allah?﴾ up to His words: ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs all intercession"﴾ (al-Zumar 39:43–44).

And He said:

﴿And they worship besides Allah that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say: "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?" Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ (Yunus 10:18). So He, glorified be He, made clear that those who take intercessors are polytheists, and that intercession is not attained by their taking them, but is attained only by His permission for the intercessor and His approval of the one for whom intercession is made.

The secret of the difference between the two kinds of intercession is this: the intercession of a created being for another created being, and his request to the one with whom intercession is made, does not depend on that one, neither in creation, nor command, nor permission. Rather, it is an external cause that moves him, like the rest of the causes that move causes. This moving cause may find, in the one moved, something that agrees with it, as when someone intercedes with him for a matter he loves and approves. It may also find something that opposes it, as when someone intercedes with him for a matter he dislikes. Then his request and intercession may be stronger than the opposition, so he accepts the intercessor's intercession. Or the opposition in him may be stronger than the intercessor's intercession, so he rejects it and does not accept it. The two matters may also conflict in him, so he remains hesitant between the opposition that requires rejection and the intercession that requires acceptance, until one of the two prevails in him by some preponderant factor. Thus the intercession of a human with a created being is like this: it is an effort through a separate cause outside the one interceded with, which moves him, even if against his will. The position of intercession with him is like that of one who intercedes by commanding another, or compelling him to act, either by force and authority, or by making him desire his intercession. So it must be that the one interceded with gains from the intercessor either a desire through which he benefits, or a fear from which his intercession wards off harm.

This is in contrast to intercession with the Lord, may He be exalted. For unless He creates the intercessor's intercession, permits him to make it, loves it from him, and is pleased with the intercessor, it cannot occur. The intercessor does not intercede with Him because the Lord needs him, nor out of fear of Him, nor out of desire for something due to Him. He intercedes with Him only as a mere carrying out of His command and obedience to Him. So he is commanded to intercede and is obedient by carrying out the command. No prophet, angel, or any created being moves by intercession or anything else except by the will of God, the Exalted, and His creation. So the Lord, glorified and exalted, is the One who moves the intercessor until he intercedes, while the intercessor for a created being is the one who moves the one interceded with until he accepts. The intercessor with a created being is independent of him in most of his affairs, yet in reality he is his partner, even if he is his slave or servant. The one interceded with needs him for the benefit he receives from him, such as help, support, and the like, just as the intercessor needs him for what he receives from him: provision, victory, or otherwise. Each of them needs the other.

Whoever God has enabled to understand and know this matter, the reality of tawhid and shirk becomes clear to him, and the difference between the intercession God affirmed and that which He denied and nullified. ﴿And whoever God has not given light, for him there is no light﴾ (al-Nur 24:40).

Others said: "Rather, the knowledge is his own, and its meaning is: I was given it on the basis of my knowledge of the ways of earning (wujuh al-makasib)." This was said by Qatadah and others.

It was also said: the meaning is, "I know that since I have been given this in this world, I have a rank and nobility with Allah."

This is the meaning of Mujahid's statement, "He was given it on account of nobility."

The Exalted said: ﴿Nay, it is a trial﴾, meaning: the blessings with which he has been provided are a trial by which We test him and an ordeal by which We examine him. They do not indicate His choosing and selecting him, nor that he is beloved to us and close to us. This is why, in the story of Qarun, He said: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and greater in number?﴾

So if the giving of wealth, strength and standing indicated Allah's pleasure with the one to whom they were given, and the nobility of his rank and his high station with Him, then He would not have destroyed those who were given more of that than Qarun was given. When He destroyed them despite the abundance of this bounty and its expansiveness, it became known that His giving was only a test and a trial, not love, approval, or choosing them over others.

This is why, in the other verse, He said: ﴿Nay, it is a trial﴾, meaning the blessing is a trial and not an honour, ﴿but most of them do not know﴾.

Then He reinforced this meaning by His saying: ﴿Those before them had already said it, but what they used to earn did not avail them. So the evil consequences of what they had earned struck them﴾.

That is, those before them had already said this statement when We gave them Our blessings. Ibn Abbas said:

"They had become insolent toward Allah's blessing when He gave them the world; they rejoiced in it, transgressed, and said, 'This is an honour from Allah to us.'"

And His saying: ﴿but what they used to earn did not avail them﴾.

The meaning is that they thought what We gave them was due to their honour before Us, and it was not so, for they fell into punishment. What they earned availed them nothing, and it became clear that those blessings were not due to their honour before Us; rather, it is that We withhold them from whom We withhold them.

Then Allah, glorified is He, refuted this false assumption of theirs by His saying: ﴿Did they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it?﴾

This second view is supported by his saying "I was given it" rather than "I obtained it and earned it by my knowledge and understanding," which indicates his acknowledgment that another gave it to him. It is also indicated by the Exalted's saying: ﴿Nay, it is a trial﴾, meaning a test and an examination.

The meaning is that this was not given to him because of his honour before Us; rather, it was given to him as a test and trial from Us, to see whether he would give thanks for it or disbelieve.

So he has acknowledged that his Lord is the One who gave him this, but he assumed it was because of his honour before Him.

Thus, according to the first interpretation, the verse includes a condemnation of one who attributes blessings to himself, his knowledge and his strength, and does not attribute them to Allah's grace and kindness. Even if they are obtained through his acquisition, his acquisition is also from His blessings. Every blessing is from Allah alone, including gratitude, for it is itself a blessing, and it is from Him, glorified is He. No one is able to thank Him except by His blessing, and his thanks are a blessing from Him upon him, as David said:

The purpose is that the state of the grateful is the opposite of the state of one who says, "I was given it on knowledge that is with me."

**(Benefit)**

It may be said: He named them "My servants" because they did not despair of His mercy, turned back to Him in repentance, and followed the best of what was sent down to them from their Lord. Thus they become among the servants of divinity and obedience.

**(Section)**

Indeed, He, glory be to Him, rejoices at the repentance of His servant when he repents to Him with the greatest joy that can be imagined, or that occurs to the mind, or that is conceived in the heart. The occurrence of this joy depends on repentance (tawbah, turning back to God), which depends on the existence of that from which one repents. Whatever something depends upon does not exist without it, for the existence of the necessitating thing without its necessary consequence is impossible. There is no doubt that the existence of joy is more perfect than its non-existence, so it is part of complete wisdom to decree its causes and its necessary consequences.

The most knowledgeable of creation about God drew attention to this very meaning when he said, in the authentic hadith:

"Were you not to commit sins, God would take you away and bring a people who commit sins, then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them."

So, if He had not decreed sins and acts of disobedience, to whom would He grant forgiveness? To whom would He show repentance? From whom would He pardon and waive His right? And how would His grace, His generosity, His forbearance and His nobility become manifest? And He is Vast in forgiveness.

How then would this attribute be left unactualized? Or how could it be realized without that which is forgiven? Who would be forgiven? Who would repent, and from what would he repent?

Had there been in the decree of sins, transgressions and violations nothing but this alone, it would have sufficed as wisdom and as a praiseworthy end.

How much more so, when the wisdoms, the benefits and the praiseworthy ends contained within this decree are beyond what can occur to the mind.

Some of the worshippers used to supplicate during their circumambulation:

"O God, protect me from sins," and they repeated this.

It was said to him in a dream: "You asked Me for protection, and My servants ask Me for protection. If I protect you from sins, then whom will I forgive? To whom will I show repentance? From whom will I pardon?"

**[Section: Is the obedient one who has not disobeyed better than the disobedient one who has turned to God in sincere repentance (tawbah nasuhah), or is this penitent one more excellent than him?]**

Scholars have differed on this.

One group preferred the one who did not disobey over the one who disobeyed and then repented in sincere repentance, and they argued with several points:

The first: The most perfect and most excellent of creation is the most obedient to God, and this one who did not disobey is more obedient, so he is more excellent.

The second: During the time the disobedient person was occupied with his disobedience, the obedient one has advanced several stages ahead, so his rank is higher than his. The best the disobedient one can hope for is that, if he repents, he begins his journey afresh in order to catch up, while the other is on a different journey. How then can he catch up with him?

They are like two men who share in earning, such that whenever one of them earns something, the other earns its like. Then one of them deliberately squanders his earnings and refrains from earning anew, while the other is diligent in earning. When the zeal of competition seizes him and he returns to earning, he finds that his companion has earned a great deal during that period. Whatever he earns, his companion earns its equivalent. How, then, can he attain equality with him?

The third: The ultimate aim of repentance is that it erases his bad deeds and makes him like one who never committed them, so his striving during the period of disobedience is neither for him nor against him. How can this striving be compared with the striving of one who is a gainer and a profiteer?

The fourth: God is displeased with disobedience and with violating His commands. During the period in which this person was occupied with sins, his portion was God's displeasure, while the portion of the obedient one was God's pleasure. God has never ceased to be pleased with him. There is no doubt that this is better than one with whom God was pleased, then displeased, then pleased again. Constant pleasure is better than pleasure interrupted by displeasure.

The fifth: Sin is like drinking poison, repentance is its antidote and remedy, and obedience is health and well-being. Continuous health and well-being is better than health interrupted by sickness, and than drinking poison from which one recovers, when it may have led to destruction or lasting illness.

The sixth: The disobedient one is in great danger, for he is caught between three things:

The first: Ruin and death from drinking the poison.

The second: Loss of strength and its weakening, if he survives destruction.

The third: The return of his strength to him as it was, or better than it; but this is remote. The first two cases are the most common, and the third is perhaps extremely rare. So he is certain of the harm of the poison and hopeful of recovery, unlike one who has not consumed it.

The seventh: The obedient one has encircled the garden of his obedience with a fortified wall that enemies cannot reach. Its fruit, blossom, greenery and splendor are always increasing and growing. The disobedient one has opened a breach in it, made a gap in it, and allowed thieves and enemies in, and they entered, ravaging it right and left. They corrupted its branches, ruined its walls, cut off its fruit, burned its surroundings, cut off its water and reduced its irrigation. When will this one return to its original state? Even if he later restores it, gathers its scattered parts, repairs what has been corrupted, opens its water channels and rebuilds what has been ruined, it will either return as it was, or fall short, or become better. But it will never reach the garden of his companion, which has remained in its freshness and beauty, rather growing and flourishing, its fruit multiplied, and its planting increased.

The eighth: The enemy's greed for this disobedient one arose only from the weakness of his knowledge and the weakness of his resolve. That is why he is called ignorant. Qatadah said: "The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) agreed that everything disobeyed God by is ignorance." Likewise God, exalted is He, said concerning Adam: ﴿And We did not find in him resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], and He said concerning others: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast of resolve among the Messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35].

As for one whose resolve is strong, whose knowledge is complete and whose faith is firm, his enemy does not covet him, and he is more excellent.

The ninth: Disobedience must necessarily leave an evil effect, and it is either total destruction, or loss and punishment, which is followed either by pardon and entry into Paradise, or by a decrease in rank, or by the extinguishing of the lamp of faith. The repentant one's work is to remove these effects and to atone for them, while the obedient one's work is to increase and raise ranks.

For this reason, the night prayer was a supererogatory practice specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), for he works toward increasing ranks, while others work toward expiating bad deeds. How can this compare with that?

The tenth: The one who turns to God in obedience travels with the totality of his deeds, and as his acts of obedience increase, his gains through them increase and grow. He is like a man who travels and earns ten times his capital. Then he travels a second time with his original capital and his earnings, and earns ten times that again. Then he travels a third time with all this wealth, and his profit is likewise, and so on. But if he slackens in the journey at the end of his affair, even once, he loses from the profit an amount equal to all that he gained, or more.

This is the meaning of the saying of al-Junayd (may God have mercy on him): "If a sincere one turned toward God for a thousand years, then turned away from Him for a single moment, what he lost would be more than what he gained." This is correct in this sense: during the period of turning away he has lost the profit of all those deeds, and that is greater than the earlier profit. If this is the condition of one who turns away, how much more so is the condition of one who disobeys and sins? In this point there is sufficiency.

**(Section)**

Another group preferred the penitent, while not denying that the first has more good deeds than him, and they argued with several points:

The first: The servitude of repentance is among the most beloved forms of servitude to God, and the most honored by Him. He, glory be to Him, loves those who repent (al-tawwabin). Had repentance not been the most beloved of things to Him, He would not have tested the most noble of creation with sin. Because of His love for His servant's repentance, He tested him with the sin that necessitates the occurrence of what He loves, namely repentance, and an increase in His love for His servant. For the penitent have a special love with Him. This is clarified by:

The second point: Repentance has with Him, glory be to Him, a station that no other act of obedience possesses. For this reason He rejoices at the repentance of His servant when he turns to Him with the greatest joy that can be conceived, as the Prophet (ﷺ) illustrated it with the joy of the one who has lost his riding animal, which carried his food and drink, in a desolate and deadly desert, after he had lost it and despaired of the means of life. This joy does not come in any act of obedience except repentance. It is well known that this joy has a great effect on the state and heart of the penitent, and its increase cannot be expressed. It is among the secrets of decreeing sins upon the servants. For the servant attains through repentance the rank of being beloved, so that he becomes a beloved of God, for God loves those who repent and loves the tested servant who repents. This is clarified by:

The third point: The servitude of repentance contains a humility, brokenness, submission, and supplication before God, and abasement before Him, which is more beloved to Him than many visible deeds, even if those deeds exceed the servitude of repentance in quantity and measure. For humiliation and brokenness are the spirit of servitude, its marrow and its essence. This is clarified by:

The fourth point: The attainment of the degrees of humiliation and brokenness is more perfect for the penitent than for others. He has shared with one who has not sinned in the humiliation of poverty, servitude and love, and he is distinguished from him by the brokenness of his heart. As in the Israelite report: "O Lord, where can I find You?" He said: "With those whose hearts are broken for My sake." For this reason, the servant is nearest to his Lord while he is prostrating, because it is a station of humiliation and brokenness before his Lord.

Consider the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he relates from his Lord, mighty and majestic, that "He will say on the Day of Resurrection: O son of Adam, I asked you for food and you did not feed Me. He will say: O Lord, how could I feed You, when You are Lord of the worlds? He will say: My servant so-and-so asked you for food and you did not feed him. Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me. O son of Adam, I asked you for water and you did not give Me drink. He will say: O Lord, how could I give You drink, when You are Lord of the worlds? He will say: My servant so-and-so asked you for water and you did not give him drink. Had you given him drink, you would have found that with Me. O son of Adam, I fell ill and you did not visit Me. He will say: O Lord, how could I visit You, when You are Lord of the worlds? He will say: My servant so-and-so fell ill and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him."

He said regarding visiting the sick: "you would have found Me with him," and regarding feeding and giving drink: "you would have found that with Me." Thus He distinguished between them, for the sick person's heart is broken, whoever he may be. The sickness must break him. If he is a believer whose heart has been broken by sickness, God is with him.

This, God knows best, is the secret of the answering of the supplication of three: the wronged one, the traveler, and the fasting one, because of the brokenness that is in the heart of each of them. For the traveler's estrangement and brokenness is something the servant finds within himself. Likewise fasting, for it breaks the carnal, animal soul's fierceness and humbles it.

The purpose is that the candle of consolation, grace and gifts descends only into the candelabrum of brokenness, and the disobedient penitent has the fullest share of that. This is clarified by:

The fifth aspect: a sin may sometimes benefit the servant more when repentance accompanies it, than many acts of obedience. This is the meaning of the saying of some of the early pious predecessors (al-salaf): "A servant may commit a sin and enter Paradise because of it, and perform an act of obedience and enter the Fire because of it." They said: "How is that?" He said: "He commits a sin and it never leaves his sight. Whether he stands, sits or walks, he remembers his sin, so it produces in him humility, repentance, seeking forgiveness and regret, and this becomes the cause of his salvation. And he performs a good deed and it never leaves his sight. Whether he stands, sits or walks, whenever he remembers it, it leaves in him self-admiration, arrogance and a sense of having done a favour, so it becomes the cause of his ruin." Thus the sin becomes the cause of the performance of acts of obedience and good deeds, and of inner states of the heart: fear of Allah and shyness before Him, lowering oneself before Him with head bowed in shame, weeping, regretful, and seeking to make amends with one's Lord. Each of these effects is more beneficial to the servant than an act of obedience that produces in him arrogance, pride, contempt for people and looking down on them. There is no doubt that this sin is better in the sight of Allah, and closer to salvation and success, than this man who is pleased with his obedience, boastful of it, and who reminds others of it, and who considers his own state a favour upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and upon His servants. Even if he says the opposite with his tongue, Allah is Witness to what is in his heart. He nearly becomes hostile to people if they do not honour him, raise him up and submit to him, and he finds in his heart resentment toward whoever does not do this for him. If he examined his soul with the closest scrutiny, he would see this hidden within it. For this reason you see him blaming whoever does not honour him or recognise his right, seeking out his faults under the guise of zeal for Allah and anger on His behalf. But if he encounters someone who honours him, respects him and submits to him, who commits many times more sins than the former, he opens the door of excuses and hope for him, closes his eye and ear to him, restrains his tongue and heart, and says: "The door of infallibility (al-'ismah) is closed for anyone other than the prophets." Perhaps he thinks that the sins of the one who honours him are expiated by his reverence, honour and generosity towards him.

When Allah wills good for this servant, He afflicts him with a sin that breaks him through it, makes him know his own worth, spares His servants his evil, lowers his head, and extracts through it the disease of self-admiration, arrogance and taking a favour upon Him and upon His servants. This sin is therefore more beneficial for him than many acts of obedience. It is like taking medicine to extract a deadly disease, as was said in the language of the situation concerning the story of Adam and his expulsion from Paradise because of his sin:

"O Adam, do not grieve over the cup of error, which was the cause of your intelligence. Through it there was extracted from you a disease that made you unfit to dwell with us, and you were clothed in the garment of servanthood."

"Perhaps your reproach has praiseworthy consequences,
and bodies are often made healthy by ailments."

"O Adam, I tested you with sin only because I love to show My grace, My generosity and My bounty upon those who disobey Me. 'If you did not sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin, then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them.'

"O Adam, you used to enter upon Me as kings enter upon kings; today you enter upon Me as slaves enter upon kings.

"O Adam, if I preserve you and your descendants from sins, upon whom shall I bestow My forbearance? Upon whom shall I bestow My pardon, My forgiveness and My repentance, when I am the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful?

"O Adam, do not grieve over My saying to you, 'Get down from it' (Qur'an 7:18). I created it for you, but descend to the abode of striving, sow the seed of piety, and let down upon yourself the clouds of tears. When love grows strong and firm and stands upon its stalk, then come and reap it.

"O Adam, I did not send you down from Paradise except that you might seek nearness to Me by ascending. I did not expel you from it to banish you from it. I expelled you from it only that you might return."

"If reproach has passed between us and you,
and our dwellings and yours have become distant,
then the affection you have known remains,
and the stumble you have suffered is mended."

"O Adam, a sin by which you are humbled before Us is dearer to Us than an act of obedience by which you feel self-satisfied before Us.

"O Adam, the moaning of sinners is dearer to Us than the glorification of those who are self-satisfied."

"O son of Adam, as long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I will forgive you for what you have done, and I do not mind. O son of Adam, if your sins reached the clouds of the sky and then you sought My forgiveness, I would forgive you. O son of Adam, if you met Me with sins as great as the earth's expanse, then met Me without associating anything with Me, I would bring you forgiveness as great as its expanse."

It is reported about some of the worshippers that he used to ask his Lord, while circumambulating the House, to preserve him from sin. Then his eyes overcame him and he slept, and he heard someone saying: "You ask Me for preservation, and all My servants ask Me for preservation. So if I preserve them, upon whom shall I bestow My favour and forgive them through My pardon? Upon whom shall I turn in repentance? Where is My generosity, My pardon, My forgiveness and My grace?" and other words of this kind.

"O son of Adam, if you believe in Me and do not associate anything with Me, I will set up the bearers of My Throne and those around it, glorifying with My praise and seeking forgiveness for you, while you are upon your bed."

In the great divine hadith of Abu Dhar: "O My servants, you commit errors by night and by day, and I forgive all sins. Whoever knows that I am able to forgive, I will forgive him, and I do not mind."

"Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Most Merciful" (Qur'an 39:53).

"O My servant! Do not despair. From you is the supplication, and upon Me is the answering. From you is the seeking of forgiveness, and upon Me is the forgiveness. From you is repentance, and upon Me is the changing of your evil deeds into good deeds."

This is clarified by the sixth aspect: the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "Except for those who repent, believe and do righteous deeds; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful" (Qur'an 25:70). This is among the greatest of glad tidings for the penitent when their repentance is accompanied by faith and righteous action, and this is the true reality of repentance. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "I never saw the Prophet ﷺ rejoice at anything as he rejoiced at this verse when it was revealed, and at the revelation of: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive you your past sins and what follows' (Qur'an 48:1-2)."

They differed concerning the nature of this replacement, and whether it occurs in this world or in the Hereafter, in two opinions:

Ibn 'Abbas and his companions said: it is the replacement of their ugly deeds with their good qualities: He replaced shirk with faith, adultery with chastity and virtue, lying with truthfulness, and betrayal with trustworthiness.

According to this view, the meaning of the verse is that their ugly qualities and evil deeds are replaced by beautiful qualities and righteous deeds, just as a sick person is replaced from sickness with health, and one afflicted by his affliction with well-being.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others among the Successors (al-tabi'un) said: it is Allah's replacing their evil deeds that they committed with good deeds on the Day of Resurrection, so He gives them, in place of every evil deed, a good deed.

The proponents of this view relied on what al-Tirmidhi narrated in his Jami': Al-Husayn ibn Hurayth narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, from al-Ma'rur ibn Suwayd, from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I know the last man to come out of the Fire. A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'Present to him his minor sins, and his major sins will be hidden from him.' It will be said: 'On such and such a day you did such and such,' and he will acknowledge it and not deny it, while he is apprehensive about his major sins. It will be said: 'Give him, in place of every evil deed he did, a good deed.' He will say: 'I have sins I do not see here.'" Abu Dharr said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ laugh until his molar teeth showed."

This is a sound hadith, but there is room for consideration in using it to support this opinion. This man was punished for his evil deeds and entered the Fire because of them, and afterwards he was brought out of it and given, in place of every evil deed, a good deed, as a charity that Allah bestowed upon him from the beginning, equal to the number of his sins. This does not mean that those sins were replaced by good deeds, for if that were so, he would not have been punished for them, just as the penitent is not punished. The discussion concerns a penitent to whom a good deed is recorded in place of every evil deed, so that his good deeds increase. Where in this hadith is there anything that indicates that?

People have taken this hadith and used it as evidence for interpreting this verse according to this opinion, and you know what is in it. However, the early predecessors (al-salaf) had depth and precision of understanding that many later scholars do not grasp.

Therefore, the use of this hadith is correct, after laying down a principle.
